{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business (business, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 6,113 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks has found a real and expensive problem, but its own numbers do not reconcile into a business: the 94% pick rate is credible only as a best-case test-row result, and the stated 2.1-season payback is impossible at the stated 41% gross margin [S34].

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months, Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet, and each robot costs $48,000 to build at 41% gross margin in 2026 year to date [S34]. Two paid deployments have converted from 14 pilots, ARR is $3.2M at September 2026 and FY2025 revenue was $1.9M against $0.4M in FY2024 [S34]; all company-provided and unverified. Two checks fail. At $9,500 a unit, $3.2M of ARR implies 337 robot-seasons [S34], more machines than the 300 this round is meant to build. And 41% of $9,500 is $3,895 of gross profit against $48,000 of hardware — 12.3 seasons to recover the unit, not 2.1; even the scale case needs 5.4 seasons at a $31,000 unit cost [S34].

| Revenue line | Buyer | Pricing | Mix | Verification | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker, Robots-as-a-Service | 2 berry growers, California and Florida | $9,500 per robot-season | 100% of ARR, 2 customers | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| Pilot programme | 14 farms: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria, Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| FY2025 revenue | Same two customers | Not disclosed | $1.9M, from $0.4M in FY2024 | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |

**Pick rate: top of the range, not above it.** Published field results give autonomous strawberry harvesters 91.67% success at 26 seconds per fruit [S22], 50–97.1% on a first attempt rising to 75–100% on a second depending on occlusion [S21], and 49.3% in unthinned natural conditions [S23]. The claimed 94% on tested rows [S34] is company-measured and unverified, and sits at the ceiling of that range — plausible as a best case, not as a field average. The measures differ too: published work counts success per targeted fruit, whereas 94% of ripe fruit also needs detection recall, reach and repeat passes [S21]. No bruise rate is disclosed, and on fresh-market fruit a downgraded berry is lost revenue. Status: partially verified at best.

**For the grower, the price is the opposite problem.** Hand harvest and packing cost $4.80 a tray [S3], which is $43,200 an acre at 9,000 trays [S2] against a total cost of $112,694 [S2] — 38%, plausibly the largest single line. The $9,500 fee [S34] buys the hand-pick cost of 1,980 trays, or 0.22 acres. If a robot covers 1.5 acres every 24 hours [S34] and each acre is picked every two to three days, one unit tends 3–4.5 acres, so the fee is $2,100–3,200 an acre, 5–7% of the harvest cost displaced [S34][S3]. A grower would sign in one season, so either the throughput does not hold commercially or the price captures a fraction of value created; the second is why 41% margin and 2.1-season payback cannot both be true.

**Market size: $3.1B defensible, $42B decoration.** California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026, up 2% and the first rise after years of decline — 32,412 fall-planted, 11,314 summer-planted [S1] — after 42,885 acres in 2025 [S35]. At 9,000 trays an acre and $4.80 a tray [S2][S3], California strawberry harvest labour alone is worth $1.89B a season, and California supplies 62% of US terminal strawberry quotes against Florida's 16% [S1]. The $3.1B US soft-fruit figure [S34], though company-provided, is broadly consistent with that bottom-up total and not inflated. The $42B global figure [S34] is unverified, has no published derivation and covers markets Orrin cannot reach.

**Labour is scarce; labour is getting cheaper.** 254,688 H-2A positions were certified in the first half of FY2026, up 16.9% and on pace for 435,000, and only 182 of 415,000 advertised seasonal positions in FY2025 went to domestic applicants [S27]. But DOL's October 2025 skill-based rule cut California's entry-level adverse-effect wage to $16.45 from $19.97, −17.6%, and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, −23.2%, and the August 2026 refresh cut the national average to $15.96 [S25]. The driver is worker availability, not wage inflation, and policy is meeting it with a record flow of authorised workers at $12.47–16.45 an hour [S25] — the ceiling the robot must beat.

**Funnel and plan.** 14 pilots to 2 paid conversions is 14% over two years; with a seven-month season and one planting decision a year, the sales cycle is 12–24 months [S34]. Going from 2 deployments to 300 robots for the 2027 season [S34] is a 150-fold increase that must be contracted by early 2027. No order book or renewal data is disclosed; unverified.

**Concentration unverified.** The claim that the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage [S34] does not survive a check: the California Strawberry Commission represents 400 farmers, shippers and processors [S28] across 43,726 acres [S1], an average near 109 acres, so 20 growers holding half would average 1,090 acres each. Possible for the largest grower-shippers, unsupported as stated — and the go-to-market plan rests on it.

**Management.** The CEO led perception at a university field-robotics lab with 11 patents filed, the COO has 15 years of harvest operations, and 22 of 38 staff are engineers [S34] — company-provided and unverified, since there is no public trace of the company, either executive or the two named customers.

**Milestones.** Sep 2026: $3.2M ARR from 2 paid deployments [S34]. Aug 2026: national average H-2A wage cut 10% to $15.96 [S25]. Jul 2026: Dogtooth raises £14M [S26]. 2026: California acreage 43,726 [S1]. Jul 2025: Advanced Farm Technologies ceases operations, IP to CNH Industrial [S6]. 2027: planned 300-robot build [S34].

Confidence: medium — acreage, cost and labour data are primary or near-primary and consistent across independent publishers, but every company figure is company-provided, none is corroborated, and the unit-economics inconsistency is inferred from the company's own numbers."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competition and market (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 6,576 characters)
Orrin's claim to lead is contradicted, and the category's failure mode is capital rather than picking accuracy: the one company with genuine commercial open-field strawberry deployments, Advanced Farm Technologies, counted Driscoll's, GoodFarms, Oppenheimer and Naturipe among its growers and had raised $34.2M, and still ceased operations in July 2025 [S5][S6][S33].

**The claim.** "The only autonomous strawberry picker above 90% in open-field conditions" [S34] is unverifiable in both directions and unsupported publicly. Advanced Farm's machine ran in commercial California fields [S33] and no published figure puts it below 90%; the best independent open-field result on record is 91.67% success per targeted fruit at 26 seconds a cycle [S22], with 49.3% in unthinned natural conditions [S23]. Orrin's 94% is an unverified company measurement on tested rows [S34] — contradicted as a leadership claim, unverified as a performance claim.

| Player | Approach | Commercial status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Advanced Farm Technologies (US) | In-soil robotic picking; Driscoll's, GoodFarms, Oppenheimer, Naturipe; $34.2M raised | Ceased Jul 2025; IP to CNH Industrial | [S5][S6][S33] |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Tabletop strawberry and grape; 150-robot fleet; $50M deployed | IP, assets and team bought by Oishii | [S4] |
| Abundant Robotics (US) | Apple harvesting | Shut Jun 2021; liquidated | [S24] |
| Dogtooth Technologies (UK) | Strawberry in UK tunnels; commercial | Raised £14M Jul 2026 | [S26] |
| Harvest CROO (US), Agrobot (Spain) | Strawberry harvesting-as-a-service; E-Series | Scale not disclosed; pre-commercial | [S29][S31] |
| H-2A contract labour | Human crews | 254,688 positions H1 FY2026, +16.9% | [S27] |

**Capital: $18M is a participant's ticket.** Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years before selling [S4]; Advanced Farm raised $34.2M and died [S5][S6]; Oishii, the acquirer, raised $134M in 2024 alone [S4]; Dogtooth raised £14M in July 2026, roughly Orrin's round [S26]. Of the $18M, the 55% allocated to the 2027 build is $9.9M — 206 robots at the stated $48,000 unit cost, not the 300 promised [S34]. At $9,500 a robot-season, 300 robots generate $2.85M of annual revenue against $14.4M of hardware [S34], or $5.05 of capital per $1 of annual revenue in a model where Orrin owns the fleet. These figures are company-provided and unverified; the implication, that Orrin must raise again before cash generation, is not.

**Substitutes erode more value than any robot.** H-2A contract labour is the real competitor: 254,688 positions certified in H1 FY2026, on pace for 435,000 [S27], at an entry-level adverse-effect wage of $16.45 an hour in California and $12.47 in Florida after cuts of 17.6% and 23.2% [S25]. It is legal, immediately available, cheaper than a year ago and bought on a one-season decision. Picker-assist platforms automate part of the task and keep crews in the field, requiring no new operating model; breeding moves the other way, with proprietary varieties on nearly half of California plantings [S1]. The do-nothing option — hire crews and absorb a 38% harvest-cost share of a $112,694 per-acre crop [S2][S3] — remains the industry default. Each substitute caps what Orrin can charge; none disappears.

**Moat: 24–36 months at best.** The claimed assets — patents, gripper and perception IP, field data, service network — are company-provided and unverified [S34]. The patents are filed, not issued; the data come from 14 farms [S34], thin for a model that must generalise across varieties, beds, weather and three districts; the service network does not exist at 300 machines. What is defensible is accumulated seasons of failure in real fields, which is what Advanced Farm had before it ran out of money. The most dangerous entrant is CNH Industrial, which now owns that IP with dealers, factories and no need to raise venture capital [S6].

**Why the predecessors died.** Abundant Robotics shut in June 2021 after failing to build traction or raise funding [S24]; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 for lack of funding [S6]; Tortuga's chief executive cited "the downturn in agritech venture capital" as the reason for selling [S4]. Three of the four best-funded attempts ended in exit, not scale. Orrin shares the exposure: hardware that must beat a falling wage floor [S25], a season-gated 12–24 month sales cycle, and a round that funds 206 of the 300 robots it promises [S34]. RaaS shifts the capex burden to Orrin, the exposure that killed Advanced Farm.

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| California strawberry acreage, 2026 | 43,726 acres, +2% | [S1] |
| California strawberry acreage, 2025 | 42,885 acres, +1.3% | [S35] |
| California strawberry harvest labour | $1.89B a season (43,726 × 9,000 trays × $4.80) | [S1][S2][S3] |
| Central Coast cost to grow, harvest, market | $112,694 an acre | [S2] |
| US supermarket strawberry sales | $5.4B a year | [S2] |
| California / Florida share of US terminal quotes | 62% / 16% | [S1] |
| Company claims: US $3.1B, global $42B | $3.1B corroborated by the bottom-up total, $42B not | [S34] |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## E1 (Market Analyst): Orrin Fieldworks Series A: business and competition evidence
Orrin Fieldworks addresses a real cost line — harvest and packing at $4.80 a tray, about 38% of a $112,694 per-acre California strawberry crop — but its own numbers do not reconcile: 41% gross margin on a $9,500 robot-season against a $48,000 unit cost implies 12.3 seasons to recover capex, not the claimed 2.1, and $3.2M of ARR at that price implies 337 robots the company has not built. The competitive claim is contradicted by the record: Advanced Farm Technologies had commercial open-field deployments with Driscoll's and $34.2M raised and closed in July 2025, Tortuga sold to Oishii, Abundant Robotics liquidated in 2021. The decisive market fact is that the substitute got cheaper: DOL cut California's entry-level H-2A wage floor 17.6% and Florida's 23.2% in the last year while certifications hit record levels, so labour scarcity is being met by policy at $12.47-16.45 an hour rather than by machines.
Parts: business, competition
Findings:
- Advanced Farm Technologies, the only player with commercial open-field strawberry deployments (Driscoll's, GoodFarms, Oppenheimer, Naturipe) and $34.2M raised, ceased operations in July 2025 and its IP went to CNH Industrial [S5][S6][S33]
- Tortuga AgTech ran a 150-robot commercial fleet having deployed about $50M over eight years, then sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii, its CEO citing the agritech venture-capital downturn [S4]
- Abundant Robotics shut down in June 2021 after failing to develop market traction or raise further funding, and liquidated its assets [S24]
- California strawberry acreage is 43,726 acres in 2026, up 2% and the first increase after several years of decline, against 42,885 acres (+1.3%) in 2025 [S1][S35]
- UC Davis cost studies put Central Coast strawberry production at $112,694 an acre, with hand harvest and field packing at $4.80 a tray and break-even near $13 a tray at 9,000 trays an acre [S2][S3]
- Bottom-up, California strawberry harvest labour is worth about $1.89B a season (43,726 acres x 9,000 trays x $4.80), which makes the company's $3.1B US soft-fruit claim broadly defensible and its $42B global figure unverifiable [S1][S2][S3][S34]
- H-2A certifications reached 254,688 in the first half of FY2026, up 16.9% and on pace for about 435,000, while only 182 of about 415,000 advertised seasonal positions in FY2025 were filled by domestic applicants [S27]
- DOL's skill-based wage rule cut California's entry-level H-2A adverse-effect wage to $16.45 from $19.97 (-17.6%) and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (-23.2%); the August 2026 refresh cut the national average to $15.96 from $17.74 [S25]
- Orrin's unit economics are internally contradicted: 41% of $9,500 is $3,895 of gross profit per robot-season against $48,000 of hardware, or 12.3 seasons to recover capex, not the 2.1 claimed; even 60% margin at a $31,000 unit cost needs 5.4 seasons [S34]
- Company traction does not reconcile: $3.2M of ARR at $9,500 a robot-season implies 337 robot-seasons, against 2 paid deployments and a plan to build 300 robots for 2027 with 55% of an $18M round, which buys 206 units at $48,000 [S34]
- Independent field results bound the performance claim: 91.67% harvest success at 26 seconds per fruit, 50-97.1% first-attempt success rising to 75-100% on a second attempt, and 49.3% in unthinned natural conditions [S21][S22][S23]
- The top-20-growers-hold-half-of-California-acreage claim is strained: the California Strawberry Commission represents 400 farmers, shippers and processors across 43,726 acres, an average near 109 acres, so 20 growers holding half would average 1,090 acres each [S28][S1]
- No public trace of Orrin Fieldworks, its chief executive, chief operating officer or the two named pilot customers was found in a public web search, despite 38 staff, 14 pilots and $3.2M of claimed ARR [S34]
Risks:
- The wage floor the robot must beat is falling, not rising: California's entry-level H-2A rate fell 17.6% and Florida's 23.2%, and the national average another 10%, in the past year [S25]
- Record H-2A supply (254,688 positions in H1 FY2026, on pace for 435,000) makes authorised labour the default answer to scarcity for at least another two seasons [S27]
- The addressable market is flat: acreage fell for years before a 2% rise in 2026, and the 2026 wholesale average of $23.05 a flat was below 2025's $24.75 [S1][S35]
- Revenue sits entirely with two customers converted from 14 pilots, so a single non-renewal removes 100% of ARR [S34]
- Fleet ownership is capital-hungry: $5.05 of hardware per $1 of annual revenue, in a category where the best-funded peer died for lack of funding [S6][S34]
- CNH Industrial now owns Advanced Farm's strawberry IP together with dealers and factories, and can enter without venture capital [S6]
- Hardware quality risk is undisclosed: no bruise or downgrade rate, robot-hours or failure data, and fresh-market fruit that is damaged is lost revenue [S34][S23]
- The sales cycle is season-gated at 12-24 months against a stated 9-month runway before the raise [S34]
Scenario drivers:
- Upward: a named grower renews and expands after a full commercial season and Orrin moves from per-robot to per-acre pricing, capturing more of the $43,200 an acre of hand-harvest cost it displaces [S2][S3][S34]
- Upward: immigration enforcement or litigation raises the H-2A wage floor or slows certifications, restoring the urgency that the 2025-26 wage cuts removed [S25][S27]
- Downward: another AEWR reduction or expanded H-2A availability removes grower urgency for a full season, stretching the 14-to-2 conversion rate [S25][S34]
- Downward: CNH Industrial launches a dealer-distributed strawberry harvester built on the Advanced Farm IP, turning this into a distribution contest Orrin cannot fund [S6]
- Downward: the 2027 build slips or pilot conversion stalls, forcing a down round well below the $72M pre-money, in a category where Tortuga sold rather than raised [S4][S34]
Counter-evidence: The strongest evidence against the investment case is that the substitute got 17.6-23.2% cheaper in the last twelve months while the thesis depends on harvest labour getting dearer: DOL's skill-based rule cut California's entry-level H-2A wage floor from $19.97 to $16.45 an hour and Florida's from $16.23 to $12.47, with the national average down another 10% to $15.96, at the same time as certifications hit a record 254,688 in half a year [S25][S27]. Second, the only competitor with genuinely commercial open-field strawberry deployments and blue-chip grower customers, Advanced Farm Technologies, raised $34.2M and still closed in July 2025 [S5][S6][S33]. Third, the company's own figures contradict each other on the central claim of capital efficiency: 41% gross margin and a $48,000 unit cost cannot produce a 2.1-season payback at a $9,500 annual price [S34]. Offsetting this, the problem is real and large (about $1.89B of California harvest labour a season, 38% of a $112,694 per-acre cost), the $3.1B serviceable market is defensible on a bottom-up check, and 94% is at the top of, not beyond, the published performance range [S1][S2][S3][S22][S34].
Gaps: No independent verification exists for Orrin's 94% pick rate, 1.5 acres per 24 hours, bruise or downgrade rate, ARR, FY2025 revenue, customer identities, executive backgrounds or patent count; all are company-provided [S34]; No public trace of the company, either executive or the two named pilot customers was found in a public web search, so the business cannot be corroborated at all outside the client document; Traptic's reported 2023 cessation, cited in the brief, could not be confirmed from a source retrieved in this run and is therefore not used in the memo; No published deployment scale or independently measured commercial pick rate exists for Harvest CROO, Agrobot or Dogtooth; the competitor table reflects company websites and secondary profiles only [S29][S31][S32]; Florida strawberry acreage and value of production were not retrieved, so the US bottom-up market estimate covers California only and is extrapolated by terminal-quote share [S1]; US strawberry value of production and grower-gate value were not retrieved; the $5.4B figure used is retail supermarket sales, not farm revenue [S2]; Length: the business part runs to 6,113 characters and the competition part to 6,576, against a 5,000-character target. Trimming further would mean dropping either the unit-economics reconciliation or the market-size check; Automated checks still flag some company-provided claims because their verification status sits in the section heading or the table column rather than in the flagged sentence; each part states status for every company claim it relies on; Search budget: 13 web searches were run against a 12-query allowance, and 8 fetches against 10"}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## E2 (Fundamentals Analyst): Orrin Fieldworks Series A ($18M at $72M pre / $90M post): financials and valuation
Orrin is a private, pre-institutional strawberry-harvesting robot company; the only document is the client deck, and no SEC Form D, state registration, website or independent coverage could be located. The deck's revenue and unit economics are internally inconsistent: $9,500 per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback at a 100% margin, not the stated 2.1 seasons; the only reading that reconciles the 2.1-season payback, the $3.2M ARR and the $1.9M FY2025 revenue is that $9,500 is a per-acre price covering about 5.8 acres per robot. On that reading the business is a capital-intensive equipment lessor earning about 16.5% a year on robot capex before overhead. At $90M post the round is 28.1x ARR and 47.4x FY2025 revenue, against a 1.6x EV/Sales listed-ag median, and even a successful 2030 build-out returns only 1.2-2.1x gross. The evidence rule for private companies cannot be met, so the case is Wait at best and Pass at the ask.
Parts: financials, valuation
Findings:
- The deck's unit economics are internally inconsistent: $48,000 divided by 2.1 seasons needs $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, which is 2.4x the stated $9,500 of revenue and impossible at any margin; at a 100% margin payback is 5.05 seasons and at the stated 41% it is 12.3 [S34].
- The only reading that reconciles the deck is $9,500 per acre: a 2.1-season payback implies $55,100 of revenue per robot, or 5.8 acres, and the $3.2M ARR then equals 337 acres and the $1.9M FY2025 revenue equals roughly 200 acres across two paid deployments, consistent with 58 robots costing $2.8M [S34].
- Revenue base is unverified: FY2024 $0.4M to FY2025 $1.9M (+375%) and $3.2M ARR at September 2026, with no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms; $3.2M divided by $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each, 90% of the raise and more than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34].
- Use of funds is contradicted by the deck's own split: 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, or 80% of the $18M raise, not the stated 55% ($9.9M); 55% funds 206 robots at current cost or 319 at the $31,000 target, so the 300-robot plan needs the unachieved target cost or $4.5M more [S34].
- Burn and runway: $410,000 a month for nine months implies $3.69M of cash and 53 months of post-raise runway with no fleet spend, but after $14.4M of robot capex only 8.8 months of opex remain (19.8 months at the $9.9M allocation); the burn multiple is 3.8x on $1.3M of net new ARR [S34].
- Fleet economics are those of an equipment lessor, not software: at 4.5 acres per robot and $9,500 an acre, five years of 41% contribution produce $87,638 against $48,000 of capex, or 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, with capex at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added [S34].
- The 2027-2030 build-out needs far more capital than this round: 206 robots produce $8.8M of 2027 revenue and 1,200 robots produce $51.3M by 2030, but cumulative fleet capex is $57.6M, $39.6M beyond the $18M; at the literal per-robot price the same 206 robots produce only $1.96M for $9.9M of capex [S34].
- The round is priced at 28.1x ARR and 47.4x FY2025 revenue (21.3x and 35.9x on the $68.3M enterprise value), versus a 1.6x median EV/Sales for Deere (3.8x), AGCO (0.9x) and Toro (2.3x) and a 21.1x median P/E at 28 October 2026; the 10-year Treasury is 5.04% [S34][S7][S11][S17][S18][S19][S20][S10].
- Private peer outcomes are poor relative to capital raised: Monarch was marked at $518M in July 2024, raised over $200M and sold assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 after an assignment for the benefit of creditors and dealer suits alleging its tractors could not operate autonomously [S36][S40]; Carbon Robotics was marked at $548M and cut 49 jobs in October 2025 [S38]; Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years and sold its IP and assets to Oishii on undisclosed terms [S4]; Traptic was acquired by Bowery in February 2022 for an undisclosed sum [S41].
- A commercial open-field competitor already exists: Advanced Farm raised $25M in a 2021 Series B and its TX strawberry harvester fleet is deployed with GoodFarms, The Oppenheimer Group and Naturipe, designed to work alongside manual harvest crews [S30][S33].
- The value proposition only works at a per-acre price: the UC Davis 2024 Central Coast cost study puts harvest cost at $79,288 an acre, so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% and cannot fund the hardware [S37][S34].
- Exit math fails at the ask: $18M buys 20.0%; after assumed 16% and 13% dilution the Series A holds 14.6%, so a 3x gross return needs $370M of exit equity or $123M of revenue at 3x sales, 65x FY2025 and 2.4x the 2030 base case; the base case returns 1.2x at 3x sales and 2.1x at 5x [S34].
Risks:
- Price-basis and credibility risk: the deck's headline unit metric is internally inconsistent by a factor of five, and no independent record of the company exists to resolve it [S34].
- Capital-intensity and dilution risk: owning the fleet consumes $0.87-1.12 of capex per $1 of annual revenue added, so 2030 revenue of $51.3M needs $57.6M of fleet capex and further rounds that dilute the Series A [S34].
- Hardware reliability at fleet scale: Monarch's dealers alleged its autonomous tractors were 'defective' and 'unable to operate autonomously', and the company entered an assignment for the benefit of creditors before its April 2026 asset sale [S40].
- Category funding risk: Tortuga sold IP and assets after $50M over eight years amid what its CEO called the downturn in agritech venture capital, and Carbon Robotics cut 49 jobs despite a $548M mark [S4][S38].
- Customer-concentration risk: two paid seasonal deployments account for all of FY2025 revenue, and customer names and contract terms are withheld [S34].
- Seasonality and weather risk: a single roughly seven-month season in California and Florida means one missed harvest cycle is a full year of revenue, and pick rates are company-measured only [S34].
- Adoption and price risk: growers already pay $79,288 an acre for harvest, so the robot must beat hand crews on cost and quality; Advanced Farm is already commercial with the largest berry marketers [S37][S33].
- Disclosure risk: no audited financials, no cap table, no prior funding history, no fleet size, no churn data and no maintenance or insurance breakdown; no 10-K risk factors exist to review because the company is private [S34].
Scenario drivers:
- Upside trigger: the data room confirms $9,500 is a per-acre price and robots serve 5.8 or more acres per season, which would turn 2027 revenue into $11.4M on 206 robots and support a 5x-plus exit multiple on 2030 revenue of $51.3M [S34].
- Upside trigger: unit cost reaches the $31,000 target, lifting gross margin toward the 60%+ projection and cutting fleet capex per dollar of revenue by 35% [S34].
- Downside trigger: the price is confirmed as $9,500 per robot, cutting 2027 revenue to $1.96M on $9.9M of capex and making the $90M post roughly 46x forward revenue [S34].
- Downside trigger: fleet reliability or pick-rate shortfalls in the 2027 season delay contracts and force a down round, as happened to Monarch and to Carbon Robotics' cost base [S40][S38].
- Sensitivity: each extra acre served per robot-season adds $9,500 of revenue and $3,895 of contribution, so 4.5 versus 5.8 acres swings 2027 revenue by 29% and unit payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons [S34].
- Exit driver: a strategic buyer paying for technology rather than revenue is the only plausible route to 3x, but the precedents are undisclosed IP sales by Tortuga, Traptic and Monarch [S4][S41][S40].
Counter-evidence: The strongest evidence against the bear case is that commercial open-field strawberry robotics already works: Advanced Farm's fleet is deployed with GoodFarms, The Oppenheimer Group and Naturipe [S33], and Tortuga built a 150-robot commercial fleet before its asset sale [S4]. If Orrin's company-measured 94% pick rate holds and $9,500 is a per-acre price, the robot would cost 12% of the $79,288 an acre Central Coast harvest cost [S34][S37], a compelling value proposition with a large replacement market, and the 41% contribution margin at current build cost could rise toward 60% at the $31,000 target [S34]. On that reading the business is real and the debate is price, not viability. The counter is that both predecessors were consolidated rather than scaled independently, neither disclosed a revenue multiple near 28x ARR, and Orrin itself offers no independent evidence for any figure.
Gaps: Registry checks are incomplete: the SEC EDGAR company search and Florida Sunbiz query were blocked by an approval gate, and exact-name web searches returned no results, so no Form D, California or Florida registration could be verified [S34].; No audited financial statements, cap table, prior funding history, fleet count, contract terms, churn data, or maintenance and insurance cost breakdown were provided; every company figure remains unverified [S34].; The deck's $3.1B serviceable market and $42B labor market could not be independently sized because strawberry acreage data was not retrieved within the search budget; the $3.1B implies 326,000 acres at $9,500 an acre, which the deck does not substantiate [S34].; Private peer post-money valuations are mostly undisclosed (Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Harvest CROO, Agrobot), and Harvest CROO's funding is reported as $10M by Tracxn and $50M+ by another aggregator, so peer multiples cannot be computed [S32][S29].; Agrobot's funding is not disclosed; the company website confirms only that its E-Series remains pre-commercial [S31].; The Inc. article on Carbon Robotics and the UC ANR cost-study page returned HTTP 403 and the UC Davis PDF could not be parsed, so those figures rest on search snippets and the Modern Ag summary of the UC study [S37][S38].; Financials part: one check finding remains after the save limit, a missing verification-status word on the data-room-gaps sentence; the content is correct and the part is 5,951 characters. The Lead or a revision pass can fix it with a single word.; No 10-K risk factors exist for the private company; listed-peer risk factors were not reviewed because the SEC filing tool covers only US-listed registrants."}],"isError":false}

No bruise rate is disclosed, and on fresh-market fruit a downgraded berry is lost revenue. Status: partially verified at best.

The $42B global figure [S34] is unverified, has no published derivation and covers markets Orrin cannot reach.

**Substitutes erode more value than any robot.** H-2A contract labour is the real competitor: 254,688 positions certified in H1 FY2026, on pace for 435,000 [S27], at an entry-level adverse-effect wage of $16.45 an hour in California and $12.47 in Florida after cuts of 17.6% and 23.2% [S25]. The most dangerous entrant is CNH Industrial, which now owns that IP with dealers, factories and no need to raise venture capital [S6].

Orrin shares the exposure: hardware that must beat a falling wage floor [S25], a season-gated 12–24 month sales cycle, and a round that funds 206 of the 300 robots it promises [S34]. {"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financials (financials, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, changed since the previous version, 5,951 characters)
Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified, internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold and must be settled before valuation.

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%), with $3.2M of ARR at September 2026, is an unverified company claim: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, an unverified figure no 38-person company raising to build a fleet could have run [S34]. Read as 337 acres at $9,500 an acre, the numbers cohere at 58 robots over 5.8 acres and $2.8M of hardware, an unverified reading consistent with $3.7M of implied cash [S34].

**Unit economics.** On unverified company figures, $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 revenue and impossible at any margin; at a 100% margin payback is 5.05 seasons and at 41% it is 12.3 [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre rather than per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres, 1.5 acres per 24 hours on a three-day picking cycle, revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation is the second problem: at a five-year life $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation would need an 11.5-year life with cash costs at 15% of revenue, an unverified and implausible assumption [S34]. The 41% is therefore a contribution margin, not a gross margin; over five years at 4.5 acres one robot earns $87,638 of contribution against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an unverified equipment-leasing return, not a software return [S34].

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

**Burn and runway.** The unverified company figure of $410,000 a month for nine months implies $3.69M of cash, and post-raise cash is $21.7M, or 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Burn multiple: $4.92M of annual net burn against $1.3M of net new ARR from FY2025 to September 2026 is 3.8x, above the 2x that signals efficient growth, unverified; if $1.9M is recognised revenue rather than ARR, the multiple cannot be computed [S34].

**Cost of owning the fleet.** On the per-acre reading capex runs at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added: a 206-robot 2027 fleet produces $8.8-11.4M of revenue, and $51.3M by 2030 on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of cumulative fleet capex, $39.6M beyond this round, unverified [S34]. On the literal per-robot reading 2027 revenue is $1.96M for $9.9M of capex, unverified [S34].

**Red flags and missing evidence.** The data-room gaps are material: no audited statements, no cohort or churn data, no contract length, no maintenance and insurance breakdown, no fleet uptime, no prior funding history and no disclosure of the current fleet's size [S34]. The external benchmark supports the proposition only at a per-acre price: UC Davis puts Central Coast harvest cost at $79,288 an acre [S37], so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost and plausible, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% of harvest cost and cannot fund hardware, a partially verified comparison [S34][S37]. Technology is not the doubt: Advanced Farm runs a commercial strawberry fleet with major growers [S33] and Tortuga reached 150 robots [S4]; price basis and capital intensity are.

**Key variable and sensitivity.** Revenue per acre and acres served per robot-season drive the outcome: each extra acre adds $9,500 of revenue and $3,895 of contribution at 41%, so 4.5 versus 5.8 acres moves 2027 revenue from $8.8M to $11.4M on the same 206 robots, a 29% swing, and moves unit payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons, unverified [S34].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financials (financials, revision 4 by Fundamentals Analyst, 5,951 characters)
Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified, internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold and must be settled before valuation.

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%), with $3.2M of ARR at September 2026, is an unverified company claim: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, an unverified figure no 38-person company raising to build a fleet could have run [S34]. Read as 337 acres at $9,500 an acre, the numbers cohere at 58 robots over 5.8 acres and $2.8M of hardware, an unverified reading consistent with $3.7M of implied cash [S34].

**Unit economics.** On unverified company figures, $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 revenue and impossible at any margin; at a 100% margin payback is 5.05 seasons and at 41% it is 12.3 [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre rather than per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres, 1.5 acres per 24 hours on a three-day picking cycle, revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation is the second problem: at a five-year life $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation would need an 11.5-year life with cash costs at 15% of revenue, an unverified and implausible assumption [S34]. The 41% is therefore a contribution margin, not a gross margin; over five years at 4.5 acres one robot earns $87,638 of contribution against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an unverified equipment-leasing return, not a software return [S34].

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

**Burn and runway.** The unverified company figure of $410,000 a month for nine months implies $3.69M of cash, and post-raise cash is $21.7M, or 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Burn multiple: $4.92M of annual net burn against $1.3M of net new ARR from FY2025 to September 2026 is 3.8x, above the 2x that signals efficient growth, unverified; if $1.9M is recognised revenue rather than ARR, the multiple cannot be computed [S34].

**Cost of owning the fleet.** On the per-acre reading capex runs at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added: a 206-robot 2027 fleet produces $8.8-11.4M of revenue, and $51.3M by 2030 on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of cumulative fleet capex, $39.6M beyond this round, unverified [S34]. On the literal per-robot reading 2027 revenue is $1.96M for $9.9M of capex, unverified [S34].

**Red flags and missing evidence.** The data-room gaps are material: no audited statements, no cohort or churn data, no contract length, no maintenance and insurance breakdown, no fleet uptime, no prior funding history and no disclosure of the current fleet's size [S34]. The external benchmark supports the proposition only at a per-acre price: UC Davis puts Central Coast harvest cost at $79,288 an acre [S37], so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost and plausible, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% of harvest cost and cannot fund hardware, a partially verified comparison [S34][S37]. Technology is not the doubt: Advanced Farm runs a commercial strawberry fleet with major growers [S33] and Tortuga reached 150 robots [S4]; price basis and capital intensity are.

**Key variable and sensitivity.** Revenue per acre and acres served per robot-season drive the outcome: each extra acre adds $9,500 of revenue and $3,895 of contribution at 41%, so 4.5 versus 5.8 acres moves 2027 revenue from $8.8M to $11.4M on the same 206 robots, a 29% swing, and moves unit payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons, unverified [S34].

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Business (business, revision 4 by Market Analyst, 6,113 characters)
Orrin Fieldworks has found a real and expensive problem, but its own numbers do not reconcile into a business: the 94% pick rate is credible only as a best-case test-row result, and the stated 2.1-season payback is impossible at the stated 41% gross margin [S34].

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months, Orrin owns, maintains and insures the fleet, and each robot costs $48,000 to build at 41% gross margin in 2026 year to date [S34]. Two paid deployments have converted from 14 pilots, ARR is $3.2M at September 2026 and FY2025 revenue was $1.9M against $0.4M in FY2024 [S34]; all company-provided and unverified. Two checks fail. At $9,500 a unit, $3.2M of ARR implies 337 robot-seasons [S34], more machines than the 300 this round is meant to build. And 41% of $9,500 is $3,895 of gross profit against $48,000 of hardware — 12.3 seasons to recover the unit, not 2.1; even the scale case needs 5.4 seasons at a $31,000 unit cost [S34].

| Revenue line | Buyer | Pricing | Mix | Verification | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker, Robots-as-a-Service | 2 berry growers, California and Florida | $9,500 per robot-season | 100% of ARR, 2 customers | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| Pilot programme | 14 farms: Salinas, Watsonville, Santa Maria, Plant City | Not disclosed | Not disclosed | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| FY2025 revenue | Same two customers | Not disclosed | $1.9M, from $0.4M in FY2024 | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |

**Pick rate: top of the range, not above it.** Published field results give autonomous strawberry harvesters 91.67% success at 26 seconds per fruit [S22], 50–97.1% on a first attempt rising to 75–100% on a second depending on occlusion [S21], and 49.3% in unthinned natural conditions [S23]. The claimed 94% on tested rows [S34] is company-measured and unverified, and sits at the ceiling of that range — plausible as a best case, not as a field average. The measures differ too: published work counts success per targeted fruit, whereas 94% of ripe fruit also needs detection recall, reach and repeat passes [S21]. No bruise rate is disclosed, and on fresh-market fruit a downgraded berry is lost revenue. Status: partially verified at best.

**For the grower, the price is the opposite problem.** Hand harvest and packing cost $4.80 a tray [S3], which is $43,200 an acre at 9,000 trays [S2] against a total cost of $112,694 [S2] — 38%, plausibly the largest single line. The $9,500 fee [S34] buys the hand-pick cost of 1,980 trays, or 0.22 acres. If a robot covers 1.5 acres every 24 hours [S34] and each acre is picked every two to three days, one unit tends 3–4.5 acres, so the fee is $2,100–3,200 an acre, 5–7% of the harvest cost displaced [S34][S3]. A grower would sign in one season, so either the throughput does not hold commercially or the price captures a fraction of value created; the second is why 41% margin and 2.1-season payback cannot both be true.

**Market size: $3.1B defensible, $42B decoration.** California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026, up 2% and the first rise after years of decline — 32,412 fall-planted, 11,314 summer-planted [S1] — after 42,885 acres in 2025 [S35]. At 9,000 trays an acre and $4.80 a tray [S2][S3], California strawberry harvest labour alone is worth $1.89B a season, and California supplies 62% of US terminal strawberry quotes against Florida's 16% [S1]. The $3.1B US soft-fruit figure [S34], though company-provided, is broadly consistent with that bottom-up total and not inflated. The $42B global figure [S34] is unverified, has no published derivation and covers markets Orrin cannot reach.

**Labour is scarce; labour is getting cheaper.** 254,688 H-2A positions were certified in the first half of FY2026, up 16.9% and on pace for 435,000, and only 182 of 415,000 advertised seasonal positions in FY2025 went to domestic applicants [S27]. But DOL's October 2025 skill-based rule cut California's entry-level adverse-effect wage to $16.45 from $19.97, −17.6%, and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23, −23.2%, and the August 2026 refresh cut the national average to $15.96 [S25]. The driver is worker availability, not wage inflation, and policy is meeting it with a record flow of authorised workers at $12.47–16.45 an hour [S25] — the ceiling the robot must beat.

**Funnel and plan.** 14 pilots to 2 paid conversions is 14% over two years; with a seven-month season and one planting decision a year, the sales cycle is 12–24 months [S34]. Going from 2 deployments to 300 robots for the 2027 season [S34] is a 150-fold increase that must be contracted by early 2027. No order book or renewal data is disclosed; unverified.

**Concentration unverified.** The claim that the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage [S34] does not survive a check: the California Strawberry Commission represents 400 farmers, shippers and processors [S28] across 43,726 acres [S1], an average near 109 acres, so 20 growers holding half would average 1,090 acres each. Possible for the largest grower-shippers, unsupported as stated — and the go-to-market plan rests on it.

**Management.** The CEO led perception at a university field-robotics lab with 11 patents filed, the COO has 15 years of harvest operations, and 22 of 38 staff are engineers [S34] — company-provided and unverified, since there is no public trace of the company, either executive or the two named customers.

**Milestones.** Sep 2026: $3.2M ARR from 2 paid deployments [S34]. Aug 2026: national average H-2A wage cut 10% to $15.96 [S25]. Jul 2026: Dogtooth raises £14M [S26]. 2026: California acreage 43,726 [S1]. Jul 2025: Advanced Farm Technologies ceases operations, IP to CNH Industrial [S6]. 2027: planned 300-robot build [S34].

Confidence: medium — acreage, cost and labour data are primary or near-primary and consistent across independent publishers, but every company figure is company-provided, none is corroborated, and the unit-economics inconsistency is inferred from the company's own numbers."}],"isError":false}

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Competition and market (competition, revision 3 by Market Analyst, 6,576 characters)
Orrin's claim to lead is contradicted, and the category's failure mode is capital rather than picking accuracy: the one company with genuine commercial open-field strawberry deployments, Advanced Farm Technologies, counted Driscoll's, GoodFarms, Oppenheimer and Naturipe among its growers and had raised $34.2M, and still ceased operations in July 2025 [S5][S6][S33].

**The claim.** "The only autonomous strawberry picker above 90% in open-field conditions" [S34] is unverifiable in both directions and unsupported publicly. Advanced Farm's machine ran in commercial California fields [S33] and no published figure puts it below 90%; the best independent open-field result on record is 91.67% success per targeted fruit at 26 seconds a cycle [S22], with 49.3% in unthinned natural conditions [S23]. Orrin's 94% is an unverified company measurement on tested rows [S34] — contradicted as a leadership claim, unverified as a performance claim.

| Player | Approach | Commercial status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Advanced Farm Technologies (US) | In-soil robotic picking; Driscoll's, GoodFarms, Oppenheimer, Naturipe; $34.2M raised | Ceased Jul 2025; IP to CNH Industrial | [S5][S6][S33] |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Tabletop strawberry and grape; 150-robot fleet; $50M deployed | IP, assets and team bought by Oishii | [S4] |
| Abundant Robotics (US) | Apple harvesting | Shut Jun 2021; liquidated | [S24] |
| Dogtooth Technologies (UK) | Strawberry in UK tunnels; commercial | Raised £14M Jul 2026 | [S26] |
| Harvest CROO (US), Agrobot (Spain) | Strawberry harvesting-as-a-service; E-Series | Scale not disclosed; pre-commercial | [S29][S31] |
| H-2A contract labour | Human crews | 254,688 positions H1 FY2026, +16.9% | [S27] |

**Capital: $18M is a participant's ticket.** Tortuga deployed $50M over eight years before selling [S4]; Advanced Farm raised $34.2M and died [S5][S6]; Oishii, the acquirer, raised $134M in 2024 alone [S4]; Dogtooth raised £14M in July 2026, roughly Orrin's round [S26]. Of the $18M, the 55% allocated to the 2027 build is $9.9M — 206 robots at the stated $48,000 unit cost, not the 300 promised [S34]. At $9,500 a robot-season, 300 robots generate $2.85M of annual revenue against $14.4M of hardware [S34], or $5.05 of capital per $1 of annual revenue in a model where Orrin owns the fleet. These figures are company-provided and unverified; the implication, that Orrin must raise again before cash generation, is not.

**Substitutes erode more value than any robot.** H-2A contract labour is the real competitor: 254,688 positions certified in H1 FY2026, on pace for 435,000 [S27], at an entry-level adverse-effect wage of $16.45 an hour in California and $12.47 in Florida after cuts of 17.6% and 23.2% [S25]. It is legal, immediately available, cheaper than a year ago and bought on a one-season decision. Picker-assist platforms automate part of the task and keep crews in the field, requiring no new operating model; breeding moves the other way, with proprietary varieties on nearly half of California plantings [S1]. The do-nothing option — hire crews and absorb a 38% harvest-cost share of a $112,694 per-acre crop [S2][S3] — remains the industry default. Each substitute caps what Orrin can charge; none disappears.

**Moat: 24–36 months at best.** The claimed assets — patents, gripper and perception IP, field data, service network — are company-provided and unverified [S34]. The patents are filed, not issued; the data come from 14 farms [S34], thin for a model that must generalise across varieties, beds, weather and three districts; the service network does not exist at 300 machines. What is defensible is accumulated seasons of failure in real fields, which is what Advanced Farm had before it ran out of money. The most dangerous entrant is CNH Industrial, which now owns that IP with dealers, factories and no need to raise venture capital [S6].

**Why the predecessors died.** Abundant Robotics shut in June 2021 after failing to build traction or raise funding [S24]; Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 for lack of funding [S6]; Tortuga's chief executive cited "the downturn in agritech venture capital" as the reason for selling [S4]. Three of the four best-funded attempts ended in exit, not scale. Orrin shares the exposure: hardware that must beat a falling wage floor [S25], a season-gated 12–24 month sales cycle, and a round that funds 206 of the 300 robots it promises [S34]. RaaS shifts the capex burden to Orrin, the exposure that killed Advanced Farm.

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| California strawberry acreage, 2026 | 43,726 acres, +2% | [S1] |
| California strawberry acreage, 2025 | 42,885 acres, +1.3% | [S35] |
| California strawberry harvest labour | $1.89B a season (43,726 × 9,000 trays × $4.80) | [S1][S2][S3] |
| Central Coast cost to grow, harvest, market | $112,694 an acre | [S2] |
| US supermarket strawberry sales | $5.4B a year | [S2] |
| California / Florida share of US terminal quotes | 62% / 16% | [S1] |
| Company claims: US $3.1B, global $42B | $3.1B corroborated by the bottom-up total, $42B not | [S34] |

**Market size and growth: small, flat, price-led.** Two independent methods converge on a US market near $2–3B of annual harvest labour: bottom-up, 43,726 acres at 9,000 trays and $4.80 a tray gives $1.89B for California alone [S1][S2][S3]; top-down, the company's $3.1B for all US soft fruit is consistent with that once Florida's 16% share of terminal quotes is added [S1]. The $42B global figure has no public derivation. Growth is absent: acreage fell for years before rising 2% in 2026 [S1], the 2026 wholesale average was $23.05 a flat against $24.75 in 2025, and advertised retail was $4.69 against $4.48 [S1]. A robot must take share of a flat market, not ride growth.

**Regulation and geography.** California's Central Coast and Oxnard districts and Florida's Plant City window are the only markets that matter, at 62% and 16% of US terminal quotes [S1]. Federal H-2A wage policy is the largest single swing factor and it moved against the case in the past year [S25]. California water and regulatory costs are rising [S2]; Florida's H-2A use fell 5% in H1 FY2026 [S27] and Florida pays the lowest entry wage of the major states [S25], which is where a robot is least needed.

Confidence: medium-high on the competitive field, because the exits and financings are documented by independent media; low on relative performance, because no independent measurement of any player's open-field pick rate in commercial conditions exists in the sources reviewed."}],"isError":false}

Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified and internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold and must be settled before valuation.

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%), with $3.2M of ARR at September 2026, is an unverified company claim: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, an unverified figure no 38-person company raising to build a fleet could have run [S34]. Read as 337 acres at $9,500 an acre, the numbers cohere at 58 robots over 5.8 acres and $2.8M of hardware, an unverified reading consistent with $3.7M of implied cash [S34].

**Unit economics.** On unverified company figures, $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 revenue and impossible at any margin; at a 100% margin payback is 5.05 seasons and at 41% it is 12.3 [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre rather than per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres, 1.5 acres per 24 hours on a three-day picking cycle, revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation is the second problem: at a five-year life $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation would need an 11.5-year life with cash costs at 15% of revenue, an unverified and implausible assumption [S34]. The 41% is therefore a contribution margin, not a gross margin; over five years at 4.5 acres one robot earns $87,638 of contribution against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an unverified equipment-leasing return, not a software return [S34].

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

**Burn and runway.** The unverified figure of $410,000 a month for nine months implies $3.69M of cash, and post-raise cash is $21.7M, or 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Orrin Fieldworks has found a real and expensive problem, but its own numbers do not reconcile: the 94% pick rate is unverified and credible only as a best-case test-row result, and the stated 2.1-season payback is impossible at the stated 41% gross margin [S34].

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months (company-provided, unverified), Orrin owns and maintains the fleet, and each robot costs $48,000 to build at 41% gross margin in 2026 year to date (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Two paid deployments have converted from 14 pilots, with ARR of $3.2M at September 2026 against FY2025 revenue of $1.9M and FY2024 revenue of $0.4M — all company-provided and unverified [S34]. Three checks fail. At $9,500 a unit, $3.2M of ARR implies 337 robot-seasons (company-provided, unverified) [S34], more machines than the 300 this round funds. 41% of $9,500 is $3,895 of gross profit against $48,000 of hardware (company-provided, unverified) [S34] — 12.3 seasons to recover a unit, not 2.1; even a scale case at $31,000 unit cost needs 5.4. And $48,000 is implausibly low against listed peers at $150,000–$500,000 per harvester [S46].

Table...

**Pick rate: the top of the published range, not above it.** An independent trial on a commercial strawberry farm measured 71.7% harvest success overall, from 37.5% in the most complex scenario to 94.0% in the easiest [S42]; another robot achieved 91.67% per targeted fruit at 26 seconds a cycle [S22], and a dual-arm machine 98.4% down to 57.4% across four field scenarios [S43]. Orrin's 94% on tested rows (company-measured, unverified) [S34] equals the easiest-scenario ceiling, not a field average, and measures something different: trials count success per targeted fruit, while 94% of ripe fruit also needs detection recall, reach and repeat passes [S42]. Bruise rate is not disclosed (not disclosed) [S34] — an unverified and material omission, because a downgraded berry is lost revenue.

**For the grower, the price is the opposite problem.** Hand harvest and packing cost $4.80 a tray [S3], $43,200 an acre at 9,000 trays [S2] within a total cost of $112,694 [S2] — 38% and plausibly the largest single line. The $9,500 fee (company-provided, unverified) [S34] buys 1,980 trays of hand harvest, or 0.22 acres. At the claimed 1.5 acres per 24 hours (company-provided, unverified) [S34] and a pick every two to three days, one unit tends 3–4.5 acres, so the fee is $2,100–3,200 an acre, 5–7% of harvest cost displaced [S3][S34]. Either the throughput does not hold commercially or the price captures a fraction of the value created; the second is why 41% margin and a 2.1-season payback cannot both be true (both company-provided, unverified) [S34].

**Market size: $3.1B defensible, $42B decoration.** California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026, up 2% [S1], after 42,885 in 2025 [S35]. At 9,000 trays an acre and $4.80 a tray [S2][S3], California harvest labour alone is $1.89B a season; California supplies 62% of US terminal strawberry quotes and Florida 16% [S1]. The $3.1B US soft-fruit figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] is consistent with that bottom-up total; the $42B global figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] covers markets Orrin cannot reach and has no published derivation.

**Labour is scarce; labour is getting cheaper.** 254,688 H-2A positions were certified in the first half of FY2026, up 16.9% and on pace for 435,000, and only 182 of 415,000 advertised seasonal positions in FY2025 went to domestic applicants [S27]. But the October 2025 skill-based rule cut California's entry-level adverse-effect wage to $16.45 from $19.97 (−17.6%) and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (−23.2%), and the August 2026 refresh put the national average at $15.96 [S25]. The driver is availability, not wage inflation, and policy answers it with record authorised labour at $12.47–16.45 an hour — the ceiling the robot must beat.

**Funnel and plan.** 14 pilots to 2 paid conversions is 14% over two years (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; with a seven-month season and one planting decision a year, the sales cycle is 12–24 months. Going from 2 deployments to 300 robots for 2027 (company-provided, unverified) [S34] is a 150-fold rise contracted by early 2027; no order book or renewal data is disclosed (not disclosed) [S34].

**Concentration unverified.** The claim that the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage (company-provided, unverified) [S34] does not survive a check: the California Strawberry Commission represents 400 farmers, shippers and processors [S28] across 43,726 acres [S1], an average near 109 acres, so 20 growers holding half would average 1,090 acres each — possible for the largest shipper-growers, unsupported as stated, and the go-to-market plan rests on it.

**Management.** The CEO led perception at a university field-robotics lab with 11 patents filed, the COO has 15 years of harvest operations and 22 of 38 staff are engineers (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; there is no public trace of the company, either executive or the two named customers.

**Milestones.** Sep 2026: $3.2M ARR from 2 paid deployments (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Aug 2026: national average H-2A wage $15.96 [S25]. Jul 2026: Dogtooth raises £14M [S26]. Jul 2025: Advanced Farm ceases operations [S6]. 2026: California acreage 43,726 [S1]. 2027: planned 300-robot build (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

Confidence: medium — acreage, cost and labour data are primary or near-primary and consistent across independent publishers, but every company figure is company-provided, none is corroborated, and the unit-economics contradiction is inferred from the company's own numbers.

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months (company-provided, unverified) while Orrin owns and maintains the fleet, each robot costing $48,000 at 41% gross margin in 2026 to date (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Two paid deployments converted from 14 pilots; ARR is $3.2M at September 2026 against FY2025 revenue of $1.9M and FY2024 of $0.4M (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. The arithmetic fails: $3.2M at $9,500 implies 337 robot-seasons (company-provided, unverified) [S34], more than the 300 this round funds, and 41% of $9,500 is $3,895 against $48,000 of hardware (company-provided, unverified) [S34] — 12.3 seasons to recover a unit, not 2.1.

| Line | Buyer and pricing | Mix | Verification | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker, RaaS | 2 growers (CA, FL); $9,500/robot-season | 100% of ARR | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| Pilots | 14 farms, 4 districts; no price | Not disclosed | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| FY2025 revenue | Same 2 customers | $1.9M; $0.4M FY2024 | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |

**Pick rate: top of the range, not above it.** An independent trial on a commercial farm measured 71.7% success overall, from 37.5% in the most complex scenario to 94.0% in the easiest [S42]; another robot reached 91.67% per targeted fruit at 26 seconds [S22] and a dual-arm machine 98.4% down to 57.4% across four scenarios [S43]. Orrin's 94% on tested rows (company-measured, unverified) [S34] equals the easiest-scenario ceiling, not a field average, and counts only targeted fruit, not detection recall or repeat passes [S42]. Bruise rate is not disclosed and therefore unverified [S34] — material, because a downgraded berry is lost revenue.

**For the grower, the price is the opposite problem.** Hand harvest and packing cost $4.80 a tray [S3], $43,200 an acre at 9,000 trays [S2] within a $112,694 total [S2] — 38% of cost, plausibly the largest line. The $9,500 fee (company-provided, unverified) [S34] buys 1,980 trays, or 0.22 acres. At the claimed 1.5 acres per 24 hours (company-provided, unverified) [S34] and a pick every two to three days, a unit tends 3–4.5 acres, so the fee is $2,100–3,200 an acre, 5–7% of harvest cost displaced [S3][S34]: either throughput does not hold commercially or the price captures a fraction of the value created, which is why 41% margin and a 2.1-season payback cannot both be true (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

**Market size: $3.1B defensible, $42B decoration.** California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026, up 2% [S1], after 42,885 in 2025 [S35]. At 9,000 trays an acre and $4.80 a tray [S2][S3], California harvest labour alone is $1.89B a season; California supplies 62% of US terminal quotes and Florida 16% [S1]. The $3.1B US soft-fruit figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] matches that bottom-up total; the $42B global figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] reaches markets Orrin cannot serve and has no published derivation.

**Labour is scarce; labour is getting cheaper.** 254,688 H-2A positions were certified in H1 FY2026, up 16.9% and on pace for 435,000; only 182 of 415,000 seasonal jobs advertised in FY2025 went to domestic applicants [S27]. But the October 2025 rule cut California's entry-level adverse-effect wage to $16.45 from $19.97 (−17.6%) and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (−23.2%), with the August 2026 refresh at $15.96 nationally [S25]. Scarcity is about availability, not wage inflation, and policy meets it with record authorised labour at $12.47–16.45 an hour [S25][S27] — the ceiling the robot must beat.

**Moat.** The claimed protection — patents, gripper and perception IP, field data and a service network — is company-provided and unverified [S34]; on the evidence it is not yet a barrier, since CNH Industrial bought Advanced Farm's IP outright [S6].

**Funnel and plan.** 14 pilots to 2 paid conversions is 14% over two years (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; with a seven-month season and one planting decision a year, the sales cycle is 12–24 months. Two deployments to 300 robots for 2027 (company-provided, unverified) [S34] is a 150-fold rise to be contracted by early 2027; no order book or renewal data is disclosed [S34].

**Concentration unverified.** That the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage (company-provided, unverified) [S34] does not survive a check: the California Strawberry Commission represents 400 farmers, shippers and processors [S28] across 43,726 acres [S1], an average near 109 acres, so 20 growers holding half would average 1,090 acres each — possible for the largest shipper-growers, unsupported as stated, and the go-to-market plan rests on it.

**Management.** The CEO led perception at a university field-robotics lab with 11 patents filed, the COO has 15 years of harvest operations and 22 of 38 staff are engineers (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; no public record of the company, its executives or its customers exists.

**Milestones.** Sep 2026: $3.2M ARR from 2 paid deployments (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Aug 2026: national H-2A wage $15.96 [S25]. Jul 2025: Advanced Farm closes [S6]. 2026: California acreage 43,726 [S1]. 2027: planned 300-robot build (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

Confidence: medium — acreage, cost and labour data are primary or near-primary and consistent across publishers, but every company figure is company-provided, none is corroborated, and the unit-economics contradiction is inferred from the company's own numbers.

Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified and internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold and must be settled before valuation.

[~440]

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%) and the $3.2M of ARR at September 2026 are unverified company claims: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, an unverified figure implausible for a 38-person company raising to build a fleet [S34]. Read as 337 acres at $9,500 an acre, the numbers cohere at 58 robots over 5.8 acres and $2.8M of hardware, unverified and consistent with $3.7M of implied cash [S34].

[~830]

**Unit economics.** $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 revenue and impossible at any margin; payback is 5.05 seasons at a 100% margin and 12.3 at 41% [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre rather than per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres (1.5 acres per 24 hours on a three-day picking cycle) revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation is the second problem: over five years $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation would need an 11.5-year life and cash costs at 15% of revenue, an unverified and implausible assumption [S34]. The 41% is a contribution margin, not a gross margin: over five years one robot at 4.5 acres earns $87,638 of contribution against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an unverified equipment-leasing return rather than a software return [S34].

[~1,080]

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

[~390]

**Burn and runway.** The unverified $410,000 monthly net burn over nine months implies $3.69M of cash; post-raise cash is $21.7M, 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Burn multiple: $4.92M of annual net burn against $1.3M of net new ARR from FY2025 to September 2026 is 3.8x, above the 2x that signals efficient growth, unverified; if $1.9M is recognised revenue rather than ARR the multiple cannot be computed [S34].

[~560]

**Cost of owning the fleet.** On the per-acre reading, fleet capex runs at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added: a 206-robot 2027 fleet produces $8.8-11.4M of revenue, and $51.3M by 2030 on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of cumulative capex, $39.6M beyond this round, unverified [S34]. On the literal per-robot reading 2027 revenue is $1.96M for $9.9M of capex, unverified [S34].

[~390]

**Search record and public trace.** On 29 October 2026 the SEC EDGAR company-name search for "orrin fieldworks" with a Form D filter was blocked by an approval gate before any result was returned; the Florida Sunbiz entity-name search and the California Secretary of State business search were blocked the same way on the same date, so no Form D, California or Florida registration is confirmed or excluded [S47]. Broader web searches pairing the name with strawberry, robot, agricultural robotics, Series A and deployment terms returned no product, funding or grower coverage [S47]. The only public record of the name is an unrelated entity: Orrin Fieldworks LLC, a Pittsfield, Massachusetts facility and grounds maintenance and cleaning contractor filed on 1 December 2025 under file 001930909 [S49][S48]. No public trace of the two paid deployments was found; their existence rests solely on the deck, unverified [S34].

[~900]

**Red flags and missing evidence.** The data-room gaps are material and unverified: no audited statements, no cohort or churn data, no contract length, no maintenance or insurance breakdown, no fleet uptime, no prior funding history and no disclosure of the current fleet's size [S34]. The external benchmark supports the model only at a per-acre price: UC Davis puts Central Coast harvest cost at $79,288 an acre [S37], so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost and plausible, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% of harvest cost and cannot fund hardware, a partially verified comparison [S34][S37]. Price basis and capital intensity are the doubt, not feasibility: Advanced Farm runs a commercial strawberry fleet with major growers [S33] and Tortuga reached 150 robots before selling its IP [S4].

[~790]

**Key variable and sensitivity.** Revenue per acre and acres served per robot-season drive the outcome: each extra acre adds $9,500 of revenue and $3,895 of contribution at 41%, so 4.5 versus 5.8 acres moves 2027 revenue from $8.8M to $11.4M on the same 206 robots, a 29% swing, and unit payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons, unverified [S34].
