arguments.markdown:
Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified and internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold and must be settled before valuation.

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%) and $3.2M of ARR at September 2026 are unverified company claims: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, implausible for a 38-person company raising to build a fleet, unverified [S34]. Read as 337 acres at $9,500 an acre, the figures cohere at 58 robots over 5.8 acres and $2.8M of hardware, unverified and consistent with $3.7M of implied cash [S34].

**Unit economics.** $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 and impossible at any margin; payback is 5.05 seasons at a 100% margin and 12.3 at 41% [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre, not per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres (1.5 acres per 24 hours, three-day picking cycle) revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation compounds it: over five years $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation needs an 11.5-year life and cash costs at 15% of revenue, unverified and implausible [S34]. The 41% is therefore a contribution margin: over five years one robot at 4.5 acres earns $87,638 against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an equipment-leasing return, not a software return [S34].

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

**Burn and runway.** The unverified $410,000 monthly net burn over nine months implies $3.69M of cash; post-raise cash is $21.7M, 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Burn multiple: $4.92M of annual net burn against $1.3M of net new ARR from FY2025 to September 2026 is 3.8x, above the 2x that signals efficient growth, unverified [S34].

**Cost of owning the fleet.** On the per-acre reading fleet capex runs at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added: 206 robots produce $8.8-11.4M of 2027 revenue, and $51.3M by 2030 on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of cumulative capex, $39.6M beyond this round, unverified [S34]. On the literal per-robot reading 2027 revenue is $1.96M for $9.9M of capex, unverified [S34].

**Search record and public trace.** On 29 October 2026 the SEC EDGAR company-name search for "orrin fieldworks" with a Form D filter was blocked by an approval gate before any result was returned; the Florida Sunbiz entity-name search and the California Secretary of State business search were blocked the same way on the same date, so no Form D, California or Florida registration is confirmed or excluded [S47]. Broader web searches pairing the name with strawberry, robot, agricultural robotics, Series A and deployment terms returned no product, funding or grower coverage [S47]. The only public record of the name is unrelated: Orrin Fieldworks LLC, a Pittsfield, Massachusetts facility and grounds maintenance and cleaning contractor filed on 1 December 2025 under file 001930909 [S49][S48]. No public trace of the two paid deployments was found; their existence rests solely on the deck, unverified [S34].

**Red flags and missing evidence.** The data-room gaps are material and unverified: no audited statements, no cohort or churn data, no contract length, no maintenance or insurance breakdown, no fleet uptime, no prior funding history and no fleet size [S34]. The external benchmark supports the model only at a per-acre price: UC Davis puts Central Coast harvest cost at $79,288 an acre [S37], so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost and plausible, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% and cannot fund hardware, a partially verified comparison [S34][S37]. Advanced Farm built a commercial fleet for major growers before reportedly ceasing operations in July 2025 [S33][S6]; price basis and capital intensity are the doubt.

**Key variable and sensitivity.** Revenue per acre and acres served per robot-season drive the outcome: each extra acre adds $9,500 of revenue and $3,895 of contribution at 41%, so 4.5 versus 5.8 acres moves 2027 revenue from $8.8M to $11.4M on 206 robots, a 29% swing, and unit payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons, unverified [S34].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified and internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold; an investor should underwrite the per-acre case and require the price basis in writing before committing.

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%) and $3.2M of ARR at September 2026 are unverified company claims: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, implausible for a 38-person company, unverified [S34].

**Unit economics.** $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 and impossible at any margin on unverified figures; payback is 5.05 seasons at a 100% margin and 12.3 at 41% [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre, not per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres (1.5 acres per 24 hours, three-day picking cycle) revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation compounds it: five-year depreciation of $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation needs an 11.5-year life, unverified and implausible [S34]. The 41% is a contribution margin, not a gross margin: one robot at 4.5 acres earns $87,638 over five years against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an unverified equipment-leasing return [S34].

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

**Burn and runway.** The unverified $410,000 monthly net burn over nine months implies $3.69M of cash; post-raise cash is $21.7M, 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Burn multiple: $4.92M of annual net burn against $1.3M of net new ARR from FY2025 to September 2026 is 3.8x, above the 2x that signals efficient growth, unverified [S34].

**Cost of owning the fleet.** Fleet capex runs at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added: $51.3M of 2030 revenue on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of cumulative capex, $39.6M beyond this round, unverified [S34].

**Search record and public trace.** On 29 October 2026 the SEC EDGAR company-name search for "orrin fieldworks" (Form D filter) was blocked by an approval gate before returning any result, as were the Florida Sunbiz entity-name search and the California Secretary of State business search that day, so no Form D, California or Florida registration is confirmed or excluded [S47]. Web searches pairing the name with strawberry, robot, agricultural robotics, Series A and deployment terms returned no product, funding or grower coverage [S47]. The only public record of the name is unrelated: Orrin Fieldworks LLC, a Pittsfield, Massachusetts grounds and facilities maintenance contractor filed on 1 December 2025 under file 001930909 [S49][S48]. No public trace of the two paid deployments was found; they rest solely on the deck, unverified [S34].

**Red flags and missing evidence.** The data-room gaps are material and unverified: no audited statements, no cohort or churn data, no contract length, no maintenance or insurance breakdown, no fleet uptime, no prior funding history or fleet size [S34]. The external benchmark supports the model only at a per-acre price: UC Davis puts Central Coast harvest cost at $79,288 an acre [S37], so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost and plausible, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% and cannot fund hardware, a partially verified comparison [S34][S37]. Advanced Farm built a commercial fleet before reportedly ceasing operations in July 2025 [S33][S6].

**Key variable and sensitivity.** Revenue per acre and acres per robot-season drive the outcome: each extra acre adds $9,500 of revenue and $3,895 of contribution at 41%, so 4.5 versus 5.8 acres moves 2027 revenue from $8.8M to $11.4M on 206 robots, a 29% swing, and payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons, unverified [S34].

arguments.markdown:
Orrin Fieldworks has found a real and expensive problem, but its own numbers do not reconcile: the 94% pick rate is unverified and credible only as a best-case test-row result, and the 2.1-season payback is impossible at the stated 41% gross margin [S34].

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months (company-provided, unverified), Orrin owns the fleet, and each robot costs $48,000 at 41% gross margin in 2026 to date (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Two paid deployments converted from 14 pilots; ARR is $3.2M at September 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $1.9M and FY2024 of $0.4M (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. The arithmetic fails: $3.2M at $9,500 implies 337 robot-seasons (company-provided, unverified) [S34], more than the 300 this round funds, and 41% of $9,500 gives $3,895 against $48,000 of hardware (company-provided, unverified) [S34] — 12.3 seasons to recover a unit, not 2.1.

| Line | Buyer and pricing | Mix | Verification | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker, RaaS | 2 growers (CA, FL), $9,500/robot-season | 100% of ARR | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| Pilots | 14 farms, 4 districts, no price | Not disclosed | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |
| FY2025 revenue | Same 2 customers | $1.9M, from $0.4M | Company-provided, unverified | [S34] |

**Pick rate: top of the range, not above it.** An independent trial on a commercial farm measured 71.7% success overall, 37.5% in the hardest scenario and 94.0% in the easiest [S42]; another robot reached 91.67% per targeted fruit at 26 seconds [S22]. Orrin's 94% on tested rows (company-measured, unverified) [S34] equals that easiest-scenario ceiling, not a field average, and counts only targeted fruit, not detection recall or repeat passes [S42]. Bruise rate is not disclosed and therefore unverified [S34] — material, because a downgraded berry is lost revenue.

**For the grower, the price is the opposite problem.** Harvest and packing cost $4.80 a tray [S3], $43,200 an acre at 9,000 trays [S2] within a $112,694 total [S2]. The $9,500 fee (company-provided, unverified) [S34] buys 1,980 trays, or 0.22 acres; at the claimed 1.5 acres per 24 hours (company-provided, unverified) [S34] and a pick every two to three days, a unit tends 3–4.5 acres, so the fee is $2,100–3,200 an acre, 5–7% of harvest cost displaced [S3][S34] — so either throughput does not hold or the price captures a fraction of value created, which is why 41% margin and 2.1-season payback cannot both be true (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

**Market size.** California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026, up 2% [S1]; at 9,000 trays and $4.80 a tray [S2][S3], harvest labour alone is $1.89B a season. The $3.1B US soft-fruit figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] matches that bottom-up total; the $42B global figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] reaches markets Orrin cannot serve and has no published derivation.

**Labour is scarce; labour is getting cheaper.** 254,688 H-2A positions were certified in H1 FY2026, up 16.9% [S27]. But the October 2025 rule cut California's entry-level adverse-effect wage to $16.45 from $19.97 (−17.6%) and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (−23.2%), with the August 2026 refresh at $15.96 nationally [S25]. Policy is meeting scarcity with record authorised labour, not rising wages; $12.47–16.45 an hour is the ceiling the robot must beat [S25][S27].

**Moat.** The claimed patents, gripper and perception IP, field data and service network are company-provided and unverified [S34] and not yet a barrier: CNH Industrial bought Advanced Farm's IP outright [S6].

**Funnel and plan.** 14 pilots to 2 paid conversions is 14% over two years (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; with a seven-month season and one planting decision a year, the sales cycle is 12–24 months. Two deployments to 300 robots for 2027 (company-provided, unverified) [S34] is a 150-fold rise to be contracted by early 2027, with no order book or renewal data disclosed [S34].

**Concentration unverified.** The top-20-growers-hold-half claim (company-provided, unverified) [S34] is unsupported: 400 commission members [S28] across 43,726 acres [S1] average 109 acres, so 20 holding half would average 1,090 each — possible, unproven, and the go-to-market plan rests on it.

**Management.** The CEO led perception at a university field-robotics lab with 11 patents filed, the COO has 15 years of harvest operations and 22 of 38 staff are engineers (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; no public record of the company, its executives or its customers exists.

**Milestones.** Sep 2026: $3.2M ARR from 2 paid deployments (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Aug 2026: national H-2A wage $15.96 [S25]. Jul 2026: Dogtooth raises £14M [S26]. Jul 2025: Advanced Farm closes [S6]. 2027: planned 300-robot build (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

Confidence: medium — acreage, cost and labour data are primary or near-primary and consistent; every company figure is company-provided and uncorroborated, and the unit-economics contradiction is inferred from the company's own numbers.

Orrin Fieldworks has a real problem, but its own numbers do not reconcile: the 94% pick rate is unverified and credible only as a best-case test-row result, and the 2.1-season payback is impossible at the stated 41% gross margin [S34].

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months (company-provided, unverified), Orrin owns the fleet, and each robot costs $48,000 at 41% gross margin in 2026 to date (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Two paid deployments converted from 14 pilots; ARR is $3.2M at September 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $1.9M and FY2024 of $0.4M (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. The arithmetic fails: $3.2M at $9,500 implies 337 robot-seasons (company-provided, unverified) [S34], more than the 300 this round funds, and 41% of $9,500 gives $3,895 against $48,000 of hardware (company-provided, unverified) [S34] — 12.3 seasons to recover a unit, not 2.1.

| Line | Buyer and pricing | Mix | Verification | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Picker, RaaS | 2 growers (CA, FL), $9,500/robot-season | 100% of ARR | Unverified (company) | [S34] |
| Pilots | 14 farms, 4 districts, no price | Not disclosed | Unverified (company) | [S34] |
| FY2025 revenue | Same 2 customers | $1.9M, from $0.4M | Unverified (company) | [S34] |

**Pick rate: top of the range, not above it.** An independent trial on a commercial farm measured 71.7% success overall, 37.5% in the hardest scenario and 94.0% in the easiest [S42]; another robot reached 91.67% per targeted fruit at 26 seconds [S22]. Orrin's 94% on tested rows (company-measured, unverified) [S34] equals that easiest-scenario ceiling, not a field average, and counts only targeted fruit, not detection recall or repeat passes [S42]. Bruise rate is undisclosed and unverified [S34], and a downgraded berry is lost revenue.

**For the grower, the price is the opposite problem.** Harvest and packing cost $4.80 a tray [S3], $43,200 an acre at 9,000 trays [S2] within a $112,694 total [S2]. The $9,500 fee (company-provided, unverified) [S34] buys 1,980 trays, or 0.22 acres; at the claimed 1.5 acres per 24 hours (company-provided, unverified) [S34] and a pick every two to three days, a unit tends 3–4.5 acres, so the fee is $2,100–3,200 an acre, 5–7% of harvest cost displaced [S3][S34] — so either throughput fails or Orrin captures a fraction of value created, which is why 41% margin and 2.1-season payback cannot both be true (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

**Market size.** California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026 [S1]; at 9,000 trays and $4.80 a tray [S2][S3], harvest labour alone is $1.89B a season. The $3.1B US figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] matches that bottom-up total; the $42B global figure (company-provided, unverified) [S34] covers markets Orrin cannot serve and has no published derivation.

**Labour is scarce; labour is getting cheaper.** 254,688 H-2A positions were certified in H1 FY2026, up 16.9% [S27]. But the October 2025 rule cut California's entry-level adverse-effect wage to $16.45 from $19.97 (−17.6%) and Florida's to $12.47 from $16.23 (−23.2%), with the August 2026 refresh at $15.96 nationally [S25]. Policy meets scarcity with record authorised labour, not rising wages; $12.47–16.45 an hour is the ceiling the robot must beat [S25][S27].

**Moat.** The claimed patents, gripper and perception IP, field data and service network are company-provided and unverified [S34] and not yet a barrier: CNH Industrial bought Advanced Farm's IP outright [S6].

**Funnel and plan.** 14 pilots to 2 paid conversions is 14% over two years (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; with one planting decision yearly, the sales cycle is 12–24 months. Two deployments to 300 robots for 2027 (company-provided, unverified) [S34] is a 150-fold rise to be contracted by early 2027, with no order book or renewal data disclosed [S34].

**Concentration unverified.** The top-20-growers-hold-half claim (company-provided, unverified) [S34] is unsupported: 400 commission members [S28] across 43,726 acres [S1] average 109 acres, so 20 holding half would average 1,090 each — possible, unproven, and the go-to-market plan rests on it.

**Management.** The CEO led perception at a university field-robotics lab, the COO has 15 years of harvest operations and 22 of 38 staff are engineers (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; no public record of the company or its customers exists.

**Milestones.** Sep 2026: $3.2M ARR from 2 paid deployments (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Aug 2026: national H-2A wage $15.96 [S25]. Jul 2026: Dogtooth raises £14M [S26]. Jul 2025: Advanced Farm closes [S6]. 2027: planned 300-robot build (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

Confidence: medium — acreage, cost and labour data are near-primary and consistent; every company figure is company-provided and uncorroborated, and the unit-economics contradiction is inferred from company numbers.

arguments.topic: Orrin Fieldworks Series A — financials and valuation, revision round 1 (dated registry and deployment search)
arguments.summary: Orrin Fieldworks claims $1.9M FY2025 revenue and $3.2M ARR against a $48,000 robot and $9,500 per robot-season, which cannot produce the stated 2.1-season payback; only a per-acre price at ~5.8 acres per robot reconciles the numbers. The deck's own use-of-funds split contradicts its 300-robot plan. At $90M post (28.1x ARR) the round is priced far above listed ag-equipment peers. Dated registry checks on 29 Oct 2026 were blocked at the approval gate, the only public namesake is an unrelated Massachusetts grounds-maintenance LLC, and no public trace of the two paid deployments exists. Evidence supports Wait at best, Pass at $90M post.
findings: Dated registry record: on 29 October 2026 the SEC EDGAR company-name search for "orrin fieldworks" (Form D filter), the Florida Sunbiz entity-name search and the California Secretary of State business search were each blocked by an approval gate before returning any result, so no Form D, California or Florida registration is confirmed or excluded [S47].

The only public record of the name is an unrelated entity: Orrin Fieldworks LLC, a Pittsfield, Massachusetts grounds, facilities and cleaning contractor filed on 1 December 2025 under file 001930909, corroborated by a Chamber of Commerce directory listing [S49][S48].

No public trace of the two paid deployments was found: web searches pairing the company name with strawberry, robot, agricultural robotics, Series A and deployment terms returned no product, funding or grower coverage [S47].

FY2025 revenue of $1.9M over two deployments implies $950,000 and 100 robots each, while $3.2M ARR at $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons or a $16.2M fleet, 90% of the raise — all unverified and mutually inconsistent [S34].

Unit economics: $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons needs $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot; payback is 5.05 seasons at a 100% margin and 12.3 at 41%, and a 41% margin including five-year depreciation is impossible [S34].
Use of funds is contradicted by the deck's own split: 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise, not 55%; the 55% line funds 206 robots [S34].

Burn: $410,000 a month over nine months implies $3.69M of cash and gives 53 months of post-raise runway with no fleet spend, but only 8.8 months after a $14.4M fleet purchase; burn multiple is 3.8x [S34].
Valuation: $90M post is 28.1x ARR and 47.4x FY2025 revenue (21.3x and 35.9x on $68.3M EV) against a 1.6x EV/Sales median for Deere, AGCO and Toro [S34][S7][S11][S17][S18][S19][S20].

Peer precedent is poor: Advanced Farm raised $25M in 2021 for a commercial fleet and reportedly ceased operations in July 2025 [S30][S33][S6]; Monarch's $518M mark ended in a Caterpillar asset sale in April 2026 [S36][S40]; Carbon Robotics cut 49 jobs at a $548M mark [S38]; Tortuga sold its IP after deploying $50M [S4].
A 2030 base case of $51.3M revenue on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of fleet capex, $39.6M beyond this round, and after 16% and 13% further dilution returns 1.2-2.1x gross on the $90M post [S34].

The per-acre reading is the only one that passes an external benchmark: $9,500 an acre is 12% of the $79,288 an acre Central Coast harvest cost, whereas $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% and cannot fund hardware [S34][S37].

Technology feasibility is documented in the field but not at venture scale: Advanced Farm's and Tortuga's fleets were real, and both ended in shutdown or an IP sale rather than an independent scaled outcome [S33][S4][S6].
risks: Price-basis risk: if $9,500 is per robot-season rather than per acre, revenue and gross profit fall roughly five-fold and the business cannot recover $48,000 of hardware per unit [S34].
Capital-intensity risk: owning a RaaS fleet consumes $0.87-1.12 of capex per $1 of annual revenue added, requiring $39.6M beyond this round by 2030 [S34].
Demand-verification risk: the two paid deployments, the sole evidence of commercial traction, have no public trace and their terms, duration and churn are undisclosed [S34][S47].

Hardware-model risk: comparable RaaS and ag-robotics peers consumed capital and were shut, sold or restructured rather than scaled — Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Monarch, Traptic and Abundant Robotics [S6][S4][S40][S41][S24].
Dilution and exit risk: two further rounds take the Series A to 14.6%, and a 3x return needs $370M of exit equity at a premium multiple with only undisclosed IP-sale precedents [S34][S4][S41].
Verification risk: no Form D, state registration, website or independent coverage could be confirmed on 29 October 2026 because all three registry lookups were blocked at the approval gate [S47].
scenario_drivers: Up: audited FY2026 accounts show $3.2M of contracted ARR at a per-acre price, with 2027 season contracts naming growers and disclosed terms [S34].
Up: unit cost reaches the $31,000 target at 500 units, cutting fleet capex per dollar of revenue by 35% [S34].
Down: the price is per robot-season, which cuts the 2027 revenue pool five-fold at the same fleet size [S34].
Down: a further equity round is needed before the 2027 season; at 16% and 13% dilution the Series A falls to 14.6% [S34].
Down: a peer discloses that autonomous open-field strawberry harvesting is already sold commercially at scale, removing the scarcity premium in the $90M post [S6][S4].
counter_evidence: The per-acre reading makes the economics coherent: $9,500 an acre is 12% of the $79,288 an acre Central Coast harvest cost, and at 5.8 acres a robot earns $55,100 a season, which does support a roughly 2.1-season payback [S34][S37].

Commercial open-field strawberry harvesting has been demonstrated by Advanced Farm with GoodFarms, Oppenheimer and Naturipe and by Tortuga with 150 robots, so the technology is not the open question [S30][S33][S4].

If the price is per acre and the fleet is owned, the model is an equipment-leasing business earning 16.5% a year on capex before R&D, sales and G&A, which can be financed with debt rather than priced as software [S34].
gaps: No SEC Form D, California or Florida registration was confirmed or excluded: all three registry lookups on 29 October 2026 were blocked by an approval gate before returning a result [S47].
No audited financial statements, revenue-recognition policy, cap table, contract terms, fleet size, uptime, churn or maintenance and insurance data were provided [S34].
The two paid deployments are unverified and have no public trace; customer names remain confidential and were not searched [S34][S47].
Private peer marks (Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Harvest CROO, Traptic) are undisclosed, so peer multiples are not computable [S30][S4][S32][S41].
The $3.1B market-size claim is unverified and was not used; the bottom-up model is built from robot throughput instead [S34].

Evidence supports Wait at best, Pass at $90M post.

arguments.markdown:
Orrin's claim to lead is contradicted, and the category's failure mode is capital, not picking accuracy: Advanced Farm Technologies, the one company with genuine commercial open-field strawberry deployments, counted Driscoll's and Oppenheimer among its growers, had raised $34.2M, and ceased operations in July 2025 [S5][S6][S33].

**The claim.** "The only autonomous strawberry picker above 90% in open-field conditions" (company claim, unverified) [S34] is publicly unsupported and contradicted as a leadership claim. Advanced Farm's machine ran in commercial California fields [S33]. Independent trials measure 71.7% overall success on a commercial farm, 37.5% to 94.0% by scenario [S42], and 91.67% per targeted fruit at 26 seconds [S22]; Orrin's 94% on tested rows (company-measured, unverified) [S34] is the easiest-scenario ceiling, not a field average. No independent commercial-field measurement has been published for Orrin.

| Player | Approach | Commercial status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Advanced Farm (US) | In-soil picking; Driscoll's, Oppenheimer, Naturipe; $34.2M raised | Ceased Jul 2025; IP to CNH Industrial | [S5][S6][S33] |
| Tortuga AgTech (US) | Tabletop strawberry; 150-robot fleet; $50M deployed | Sold to Oishii | [S4] |
| Dogtooth (UK) | Strawberry, tunnels; commercial | Raised £14M, Jul 2026 | [S26] |
| Harvest CROO (US), Agrobot (Spain) | Strawberry as a service; E-Series | Pre-commercial; scale not disclosed | [S29][S31] |

**Capital: $18M is a participant's ticket.** Tortuga deployed $50M before selling [S4], Advanced Farm raised $34.2M and closed [S5][S6], and Dogtooth raised £14M in July 2026, about Orrin's round [S26]. Strawberry harvesters list at $150,000–$500,000 with 24–36-month paybacks [S46]; Harvest CROO is quoted at $300–500 an acre [S44] and robotic apple harvest models break even at $248 an acre a year [S45], against Orrin's $2,100–3,200 an acre and $48,000 unit cost (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. 55% of the $18M is $9.9M — 206 robots at $48,000, not the 300 promised (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

**Substitutes erode more value than any robot.** H-2A labour is the real competitor: 254,688 positions certified in H1 FY2026, on pace for 435,000 [S27], at $16.45 an hour entry in California and $12.47 in Florida after cuts of 17.6% and 23.2% [S25] — legal, immediately available, cheaper than a year ago, bought on a one-season decision. Picker-assist platforms and proprietary varieties, on nearly half of California plantings [S1], erode value without a new operating model. The do-nothing default — hire crews and absorb a 38% harvest share of a $112,694 crop [S2][S3] — remains. Each caps what Orrin can charge; none disappears.

**Moat: 24–36 months at best.** Patents, gripper and perception IP, field data and a service network are company-provided and unverified [S34]: patents filed, not issued; data from 14 farms (company-provided, unverified) [S34]; no service network at 300 machines. What is defensible is accumulated seasons in real fields, which Advanced Farm had before it ran out of money. The most dangerous entrant is CNH Industrial, which owns that IP with dealers and factories and no need to raise venture capital [S6].

**Why the predecessors died.** Advanced Farm closed in July 2025 for lack of funding [S6]; Abundant Robotics shut in June 2021 without traction or funding [S24]; Tortuga's chief executive cited "the downturn in agritech venture capital" [S4]. Three of the four best-funded attempts ended in exit, not scale, and Orrin shares the exposure: hardware that must beat a falling wage floor [S25], a season-gated sales cycle, and a round funding 206 of 300 promised robots (company-provided, unverified) [S34].

| Measure | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| California strawberry acreage, 2026 | 43,726 acres, +2% | [S1] |
| California acreage, 2025 | 42,885 acres | [S35] |
| California harvest labour | $1.89B a season (43,726 × 9,000 trays × $4.80) | [S1][S2][S3] |
| Central Coast cost per acre | $112,694 | [S2] |

{"content":[{"type":"text","text":"## Financials (financials, revision 6 by Fundamentals Analyst, 6,038 characters)
Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified and internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold; an investor should underwrite the per-acre case and require the price basis in writing before committing.

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%) and $3.2M of ARR at September 2026 are unverified company claims: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, implausible for a 38-person company, unverified [S34].

**Unit economics.** $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 and impossible at any margin on unverified figures; payback is 5.05 seasons at a 100% margin and 12.3 at 41% [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre, not per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres (1.5 acres per 24 hours, three-day picking cycle) revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation compounds it: five-year depreciation of $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation needs an 11.5-year life, unverified and implausible [S34]. The 41% is a contribution margin, not a gross margin: one robot at 4.5 acres earns $87,638 over five years against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an unverified equipment-leasing return [S34].

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

**Burn and runway.** The unverified $410,000 monthly net burn over nine months implies $3.69M of cash; post-raise cash is $21.7M, 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Burn multiple: $4.92M of annual net burn against $1.3M of net new ARR from FY2025 to September 2026 is 3.8x, above the 2x that signals efficient growth, unverified [S34].

**Cost of owning the fleet.** Fleet capex runs at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added: $51.3M of 2030 revenue on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of cumulative capex, $39.6M beyond this round, unverified [S34].

**Search record and public trace.** On 29 October 2026 the SEC EDGAR company-name search for "orrin fieldworks" (Form D filter) was blocked by an approval gate before returning any result, as were the Florida Sunbiz entity-name search and the California Secretary of State business search that day, so no Form D, California or Florida registration is confirmed or excluded [S47]. Web searches pairing the name with strawberry, robot, agricultural robotics, Series A and deployment terms returned no product, funding or grower coverage [S47]. The only public record of the name is unrelated: Orrin Fieldworks LLC, a Pittsfield, Massachusetts grounds and facilities maintenance contractor filed on 1 December 2025 under file 001930909 [S49][S48]. No public trace of the two paid deployments was found; they rest solely on the deck, unverified [S34].

**Red flags and missing evidence.** The data-room gaps are material and unverified: no audited statements, no cohort or churn data, no contract length, no maintenance or insurance breakdown, no fleet uptime, no prior funding history or fleet size [S34]. The external benchmark supports the model only at a per-acre price: UC Davis puts Central Coast harvest cost at $79,288 an acre [S37], so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost and plausible, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% and cannot fund hardware, a partially verified comparison [S34][S37]. Advanced Farm built a commercial fleet before reportedly ceasing operations in July 2025 [S33][S6].

**Key variable and sensitivity.** Revenue per acre and acres per robot-season drive the outcome: each extra acre adds $9,500 of revenue and $3,895 of contribution at 41%, so 4.5 versus 5.8 acres moves 2027 revenue from $8.8M to $11.4M on 206 robots, a 29% swing, and payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons, unverified [S34].

| ARR (Sep 2026) | $3.2M | 337 robot-seasons at $48k = $16.2M fleet | Unverified, inconsistent | S34 |
| Price per robot-season | $9,500 | 2.1-season payback needs $22,857 a year | Contradicted | S34 |
| Unit cost | $48,000 ($31,000 at 500 units) | 5.05-season payback at 100% margin | Unverified | S34 |

| Net burn / runway | $410k a month; 9 months | implies $3.69M of cash | Unverified | S34 |

arguments.topic: Orrin Fieldworks Series A — revision round 1: business and competition, with robotic-harvest pricing and independent field-performance evidence
arguments.summary: Revision of the business and competition parts. Added independent commercial-farm pick-rate evidence (71.7% overall, 37.5%-94.0% by scenario) that places the deck's 94% at the easiest-scenario ceiling, and published robotic-harvest pricing ($150K-$500K per machine, $300-500/acre quoted, $248/acre-year academic break-even) against Orrin's $48,000 unit and $2,100-3,200/acre. Both parts now pass the check at under 5,000 characters with sentence-level verification labels on every company claim.
findings: Orrin's own numbers contradict each other: 41% x $9,500 = $3,895 gross profit per robot-season against $48,000 of hardware, 12.3 seasons to recover a unit rather than 2.1; $3.2M of ARR at $9,500 implies 337 robot-seasons against 2 paid deployments; and 55% of $18M buys 206 robots at $48,000, not 300 [S34].

An independent trial of a small autonomous strawberry robot on a commercial farm measured 71.7% harvest success overall, with 37.5% in the most complex scenario and 94.0% in the easiest - so Orrin's 94% on tested rows equals the easiest-scenario ceiling, not a field average [S42].

Peer-reviewed field evaluations report 91.67% success per targeted fruit at 26 seconds a cycle and 98.4% down to 57.4% across four field scenarios, confirming that published performance is scenario-dependent and measured per targeted fruit [S22][S43].

Advanced Farm Technologies, the only genuinely commercial open-field strawberry deployment, counted Driscoll's, GoodFarms, Oppenheimer and Naturipe among its growers and had raised $34.2M, yet ceased operations in July 2025 with its IP going to CNH Industrial [S5][S6][S33].

Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii, and Abundant Robotics shut in June 2021 - three of the four best-funded harvest-robotics attempts exited rather than scaled [S4][S24].

Capital required is well above this round: Tortuga deployed $50M before selling, Advanced Farm raised $34.2M and closed, and Dogtooth raised GBP 14M in July 2026, roughly Orrin's Series A [S4][S5][S6][S26].

Published robotic-harvest pricing: strawberry harvesters list at $150,000-$500,000 with quoted 24-36-month paybacks; Harvest CROO is quoted on a $300-500 per-acre service model; modelled robotic apple harvest breaks even at $248 per acre per year - against Orrin's $48,000 unit cost and $2,100-3,200 per acre [S46][S44][S45][S34].

H-2A supply hit 254,688 certified positions in H1 FY2026, up 16.9% and on pace for 435,000, while the October 2025 rule cut the California entry-level adverse-effect wage from $19.97 to $16.45 (-17.6%) and Florida's from $16.23 to $12.47 (-23.2%), with the national average at $15.96 after the August 2026 refresh [S27][S25].

California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026, up 2% after 42,885 in 2025; at 9,000 trays an acre and $4.80 a tray, California harvest labour alone is worth $1.89B a season, which makes the deck's $3.1B US soft-fruit figure defensible but leaves the $42B global figure with no published derivation [S1][S35][S2][S3][S34].
Grower cost structure: harvest and packing at $4.80 a tray, 9,000 trays an acre and a $112,694 per-acre total put harvest at about 38% of cost, plausibly the largest single line [S2][S3].

The concentration claim that the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage is unsupported: the California Strawberry Commission's 400 farmers, shippers and processors across 43,726 acres average about 109 acres, so 20 growers holding half would average 1,090 acres each [S28][S1][S34].
No bruise rate, robot-hours or repeat-pass performance is disclosed, and there is no public trace of Orrin, its executives or its two named customers [S34].
risks: Wage deflation removes the value proposition: entry-level H-2A wages fell 17.6% in California and 23.2% in Florida, so the human substitute is cheaper than a year ago [S25].
Capital intensity of a Robots-as-a-Service model that owns the fleet: better-funded peers with commercial deployments still ran out of money [S4][S5][S6].
Incumbent entry: CNH Industrial now owns Advanced Farm's IP plus dealers and factories, and can enter without venture funding [S6].
Performance risk: the 94% pick rate is unverified, bruise rate is undisclosed, and independent commercial-farm trials average well below the claim [S34][S42].
Adoption risk: 14 pilots produced 2 paid deployments, and the plan needs 300 robots contracted by early 2027 with no order book disclosed [S34].
Market risk: California acreage is flat to slightly up and the 2026 wholesale price fell, so growth must come from share capture [S1].
scenario_drivers: Up: independent field validation above 90% on ripe fruit with a disclosed bruise rate, and a signed 2027 order book covering a material share of the 300-robot plan [S34].
Up: tighter immigration enforcement or an H-2A wage reversal that raises the labour cost floor the robot must beat [S25][S27].
Up: acquisition interest from an OEM seeking harvest IP, as CNH Industrial showed with Advanced Farm [S6].
Down: another season without conversion beyond two paid deployments, forcing a down round or bridge [S34].
Down: further adverse-effect wage cuts or expanded H-2A certification, widening the price gap the robot must close [S25][S27].
Down: a credible independent measurement showing field pick rates in the 40-70% range on ripe fruit, which would invalidate the performance claim [S42][S43].
arguments.counter_evidence: The strongest evidence against a negative read: the labour pool being displaced is large and real - $1.89B of California strawberry harvest labour alone, about 38% of a $112,694 per-acre cost - and 94% success was actually achieved in the easiest commercial-farm scenario, so the performance claim is not physically implausible [S1][S2][S3][S42]. If 94% holds on ripe fruit with acceptable bruising, Orrin's $2,100-3,200 per acre captures only 5-7% of the harvest cost it displaces, leaving enough pricing headroom to reach a viable payback without the deck's arithmetic [S34][S3]. Record H-2A certification also signals structural demand for harvest labour rather than its disappearance [S27].
gaps: No public trace of Orrin Fieldworks, its executives or its two named customers; every company figure rests on the deck alone [S34].
No bruise rate, robot-hours per acre, repeat-pass performance or renewal data disclosed [S34].

Independent commercial-field evidence comes from journal abstracts (full texts returned HTTP 403): 71.7% overall at a commercial farm [S42], 91.67% per targeted fruit [S22], 98.4%-57.4% across scenarios [S43].
Per-acre pricing evidence is thin and low-confidence: the $300-500/acre figure for Harvest CROO comes from a directory listing, not a vendor rate card [S44].
Traptic's 2023 exit could not be verified in this run; Florida strawberry acreage was not retrieved.
Both parts pass the automated check; business is 4,995 characters and competition 4,963, within the 5,000 target.

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months (company-provided, unverified), Orrin owns the fleet, and each robot costs $48,000 at 41% gross margin in 2026 to date (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. - Use of funds is contradicted by the deck's own split: 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise, not 55%; the 55% line funds 206 robots [S34].
- Burn: $410,000 a month over nine months implies $3.69M of cash and gives 53 months of post-raise runway with no fleet spend, but only 8.8 months after a $14.4M fleet purchase; burn multiple is 3.8x [S34].
- Valuation: $90M post is 28.1x ARR and 47.4x FY2025 revenue (21.3x and 35.9x on $68.3M EV) against a 1.6x EV/Sales median for Deere, AGCO and Toro [S34][S7][S11][S17][S18][S19][S20].

Risks:
- Price-basis risk: if $9,500 is per robot-season rather than per acre, revenue and gross profit fall roughly five-fold and the business cannot recover $48,000 of hardware per unit [S34].
- Capital-intensity risk: owning a RaaS fleet consumes $0.87-1.12 of capex per $1 of annual revenue added, requiring $39.6M beyond this round by 2030 [S34].
- Demand-verification risk: the two paid deployments, the sole evidence of commercial traction, have no public trace and their terms, duration and churn are undisclosed [S34][S47].
- Hardware-model risk: comparable RaaS and ag-robotics peers consumed capital and were shut, sold or restructured rather than scaled — Advanced Farm, Tortuga, Monarch, Traptic and Abundant Robotics [S6][S4][S40][S41][S24].

- An independent trial of a small autonomous strawberry robot on a commercial farm measured 71.7% harvest success overall, with 37.5% in the most complex scenario and 94.0% in the easiest - so Orrin's 94% on tested rows equals the easiest-scenario ceiling, not a field average [S42].
- Peer-reviewed field evaluations report 91.67% success per targeted fruit at 26 seconds a cycle and 98.4% down to 57.4% across four field scenarios, confirming that published performance is scenario-dependent and measured per targeted fruit [S22][S43].
- Advanced Farm Technologies, the only genuinely commercial open-field strawberry deployment, counted Driscoll's, GoodFarms, Oppenheimer and Naturipe among its growers and had raised $34.2M, yet ceased operations in July 2025 with its IP going to CNH Industrial [S5][S6][S33].
- Tortuga AgTech sold its IP, assets and engineering team to Oishii, and Abundant Robotics shut in June 2021 - three of the four best-funded harvest-robotics attempts exited rather than scaled [S4][S24].
- Capital required is well above this round: Tortuga deployed $50M before selling, Advanced Farm raised $34.2M and closed, and Dogtooth raised GBP 14M in July 2026, roughly Orrin's Series A [S4][S5][S6][S26].
- Published robotic-harvest pricing: strawberry harvesters list at $150,000-$500,000 with quoted 24-36-month paybacks; Harvest CROO is quoted on a $300-500 per-acre service model; modelled robotic apple harvest breaks even at $248 per acre per year - against Orrin's $48,000 unit cost and $2,100-3,200 per acre [S46][S44][S45][S34].
- H-2A supply hit 254,688 certified positions in H1 FY2026, up 16.9% and on pace for 435,000, while the October 2025 rule cut the California entry-level adverse-effect wage from $19.97 to $16.45 (-17.6%) and Florida's from $16.23 to $12.47 (-23.2%), with the national average at $15.96 after the August 2026 refresh [S27][S25].
- California farms 43,726 strawberry acres in 2026, up 2% after 42,885 in 2025; at 9,000 trays an acre and $4.80 a tray, California harvest labour alone is worth $1.89B a season, which makes the deck's $3.1B US soft-fruit figure defensible but leaves the $42B global figure with no published derivation [S1][S35][S2][S3][S34].
- Grower cost structure: harvest and packing at $4.80 a tray, 9,000 trays an acre and a $112,694 per-acre total put harvest at about 38% of cost, plausibly the largest single line [S2][S3].
- The concentration claim that the top 20 growers farm over half of California acreage is unsupported: the California Strawberry Commission's 400 farmers, shippers and processors across 43,726 acres average about 109 acres, so 20 growers holding half would average 1,090 acres each [S28][S1][S34].
- No bruise rate, robot-hours or repeat-pass performance is disclosed, and there is no public trace of Orrin, its executives or its two named customers [S34].

- Capital intensity of a Robots-as-a-Service model that owns the fleet: better-funded peers with commercial deployments still ran out of money [S4][S5][S6].
- Incumbent entry: CNH Industrial now owns Advanced Farm's IP plus dealers and factories, and can enter without venture funding [S6].

- Up: tighter immigration enforcement or an H-2A wage reversal that raises the labour cost floor the robot must beat [S25][S27].
- Up: acquisition interest from an OEM seeking harvest IP, as CNH Industrial showed with Advanced Farm [S6].
- Down: another season without conversion beyond two paid deployments, forcing a down round or bridge [S34].
- Down: further adverse-effect wage cuts or expanded H-2A certification, widening the price gap the robot must close [S25][S27].

## Orrin Fieldworks — Series A memo: **Pass** (zero position)

**Rating:** Pass · **Terms:** $18M at $72M pre-money / $90M post (20.0% for $18M) · **Confidence:** low · **Horizon:** to February 2027 contract renewals

**Thesis (two sentences).** The problem Orrin is aimed at is real — California's 43,726 strawberry acres carry harvest and packing costs of $4.80 a tray, 38% of a $112,694 per-acre crop, and the $3.1B US soft-fruit labour market checks out bottom-up at $1.89B in California alone. But the company's own arithmetic does not reconcile: $48,000 of hardware against $9,500 of revenue per robot-season is a 5.05-season payback at a 100% margin and 12.3 seasons at the stated 41%, not the claimed 2.1; $3.2M of ARR implies 337 robot-seasons against two paid deployments; and the ask is 28.1x unverified ARR (35.9x FY2025 revenue) against 1.6x for listed ag-equipment peers.

**Main risks**
- **Price basis (fatal).** The deck may be pricing a per-acre service as a per-robot rental and never says which. The only reading that reconciles the 2.1-season payback, $3.2M ARR and $1.9M FY2025 revenue is $9,500 **per acre** over ~5.8 acres per robot — an inference the company has not confirmed.
- **The substitute got cheaper.** California's entry-level H-2A wage fell 17.6% to $16.45 an hour and Florida's 23.2% to $12.47 (national average $15.96), on 254,688 certifications in H1 FY2026, on pace for 435,000. A robot now has to beat a falling wage floor.
- **Category capital failure.** Advanced Farm Technologies — $34.2M raised, with Driscoll's, Oppenheimer and Naturipe as growers — ceased operations in July 2025, its IP going to CNH Industrial. Tortuga AgTech sold to Oishii after deploying $50M; Monarch Tractor, marked at $518M, sold assets to Caterpillar in April 2026 after an assignment for creditors. Orrin's $18M is a fraction of either.
- **Performance, concentration, use of funds.** The 94% claim equals the top of the published range (91.67% per targeted fruit, 49.3% in unthinned natural conditions); no bruise rate, robot-hours or uptime is disclosed; two paid customers carry 100% of revenue; and 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise, not the stated 55% (55% buys 206).

Every company figure remains unverified.

**Scenario range:** base 1.2x, bull 2.1x, bear 0.1–0.3x gross — and the base and bull cases need $39.6M of 2027–2030 fleet capex that the round does not fund.

**The one diligence question:** *What is the contracted price per acre harvested, and the documented acres one robot serves in a season?* That single item swings 2027 revenue 5.8x, from $1.96M on 206 robots at $9,500 per robot-season to $11.4M at $9,500 per acre over 5.8 acres, and with it unit payback. Resolve it from signed 2027 grower contracts, invoices from the two paid deployments and 2026 robot-hour telematics; if the contracts show a per-robot price, $90M post is unsupportable.

None of these changes the Pass.

## Executive summary

**Pass.** Meridian should decline $18M at $72M pre-money ($90M post): the deck's figures do not reconcile, no independent record of the company could be found, and the ask is 28.1x unverified ARR against 1.6x for listed ag-equipment peers [S34][S7][S18][S20]. The problem is real: California's 43,726 strawberry acres [S1] carry harvest and packing cost of $4.80 a tray, 38% of a $112,694 per-acre crop [S2][S3], and the unverified $3.1B US soft-fruit labour market checks out bottom-up at $1.89B in California [S1][S2][S3]. **Positives:** a large, verifiable cost line [S2][S3]; a defensible US market [S1][S2]; performance at the top of the published range [S22]. **Risks:** the price basis swings unverified 2027 revenue five-fold, from $11.4M to $1.96M [S34]; the substitute got 17.6-23.2% cheaper, with California's entry H-2A wage at $16.45 and Florida's at $12.47 [S25]; Advanced Farm, the best-funded commercial player with $34.2M raised, ceased operations in July 2025 [S5][S6][S33]. Orrin Fieldworks has a real problem, but its own numbers do not reconcile: the 94% pick rate is unverified and credible only as a best-case test-row result, and the 2.1-season payback is impossible at the stated 41% gross margin [S34].

**Model and unit economics.** A track-mounted harvester sold as Robots-as-a-Service: the grower pays $9,500 per robot-season of about seven months (company-provided, unverified), Orrin owns the fleet, and each robot costs $48,000 at 41% gross margin in 2026 to date (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. Two paid deployments converted from 14 pilots; ARR is $3.2M at September 2026, against FY2025 revenue of $1.9M and FY2024 of $0.4M (company-provided, unverified) [S34]. The arithmetic fails: $3.2M at $9,500 implies 337 robot-seasons (company-provided, unverified) [S34], more than the 300 this round funds, and 41% of $9,500 gives $3,895 against $48,000 of hardware (company-provided, unverified) [S34] — 12.3 seasons to recover a unit, not 2.1.

## Financials

Orrin's unit economics do not reconcile: $9,500 of revenue per robot-season against a $48,000 robot implies a 5.1-season payback even at a 100% margin, so the company's 2.1-season payback and its per-robot price can both be true only if $9,500 is a per-acre price covering 5.8 acres per robot, an unverified and internally inconsistent company claim [S34]. That basis moves 2027 revenue five-fold; an investor should underwrite the per-acre case and require the price basis in writing before committing.

**Revenue base.** The ramp from $0.4M in FY2024 to $1.9M in FY2025 (+375%) and $3.2M of ARR at September 2026 are unverified company claims: no audited accounts, revenue-recognition policy or contract terms were provided, so recognised, contracted and annualised revenue cannot be separated [S34]. $3.2M ÷ $9,500 is 337 robot-seasons, a $16.2M fleet at $48,000 each and 90% of the raise, unverified and larger than the 300 robots it is meant to fund [S34]. FY2025's $1.9M over two paid deployments is $950,000 each, or 100 robots per deployment, implausible for a 38-person company, unverified [S34].

**Unit economics.** $48,000 ÷ 2.1 seasons requires $22,857 of annual cash flow per robot, 2.4x the stated $9,500 and impossible at any margin on unverified figures; payback is 5.05 seasons at a 100% margin and 12.3 at 41% [S34]. A 2.1-season payback reconciles only at $55,100 of revenue per robot, 5.8 acres at $9,500 an acre, the unverified inference that the price is per acre, not per robot [S34]. At 4.5 acres (1.5 acres per 24 hours, three-day picking cycle) revenue is $42,750 and contribution $17,528, a 2.7-season payback, unverified [S34]. Depreciation compounds it: five-year depreciation of $9,600 a year is 101% of the literal $9,500 revenue, so a 41% margin including depreciation needs an 11.5-year life, unverified and implausible [S34]. The 41% is a contribution margin, not a gross margin: one robot at 4.5 acres earns $87,638 over five years against $48,000 of capex, 16.5% a year before R&D, sales and G&A, an unverified equipment-leasing return [S34].

**Use of funds.** 300 robots at $48,000 is $14.4M, 80% of the raise rather than the stated 55% ($9.9M), contradicted by the deck's own split; 55% buys 206 robots at today's cost or 319 at the $31,000 target [S34]. The 300-robot plan therefore depends on a 35% cost reduction the deck calls a target, or on $4.5M more than allocated, unverified [S34].

**Burn and runway.** The unverified $410,000 monthly net burn over nine months implies $3.69M of cash; post-raise cash is $21.7M, 53 months at today's burn with no fleet spend [S34]. After $14.4M of robot capex $3.6M remains, 8.8 months of opex; at the $9.9M allocation $8.1M remains, 19.8 months, unverified [S34]. Burn multiple: $4.92M of annual net burn against $1.3M of net new ARR from FY2025 to September 2026 is 3.8x, above the 2x that signals efficient growth, unverified [S34].

**Cost of owning the fleet.** Fleet capex runs at 0.87-1.12x annual revenue added: $51.3M of 2030 revenue on 1,200 robots needs $57.6M of cumulative capex, $39.6M beyond this round, unverified [S34].

**Search record and public trace.** On 29 October 2026 the SEC EDGAR company-name search for "orrin fieldworks" (Form D filter) was blocked by an approval gate before returning any result, as were the Florida Sunbiz entity-name search and the California Secretary of State business search that day, so no Form D, California or Florida registration is confirmed or excluded [S47]. Web searches pairing the name with strawberry, robot, agricultural robotics, Series A and deployment terms returned no product, funding or grower coverage [S47]. The only public record of the name is unrelated: Orrin Fieldworks LLC, a Pittsfield, Massachusetts grounds and facilities maintenance contractor filed on 1 December 2025 under file 001930909 [S49][S48]. No public trace of the two paid deployments was found; they rest solely on the deck, unverified [S34].

**Red flags and missing evidence.** The data-room gaps are material and unverified: no audited statements, no cohort or churn data, no contract length, no maintenance or insurance breakdown, no fleet uptime, no prior funding history or fleet size [S34]. The external benchmark supports the model only at a per-acre price: UC Davis puts Central Coast harvest cost at $79,288 an acre [S37], so $9,500 an acre is 12% of harvest cost and plausible, while $9,500 per robot over 4.5 acres is 2.7% and cannot fund hardware, a partially verified comparison [S34][S37]. Signposts: $11.4M of unverified 2027 revenue and a unit cost below $35,000 [S34].

**Base (40%).** Per-acre pricing at 4.5 acres per robot, 206 robots deliver $8.8M of unverified 2027 revenue and $51.3M by 2030, and an exit at 3x sales values the Series A's 14.6% at $22.5M, a 1.2x gross MOIC [S34]. Signposts: $8.8M of unverified 2027 revenue and a 2028 Series B [S34].

**Bear (45%).** The price is confirmed as per robot, unverified 2027 revenue is $1.96M on $9.9M of capex, the 2028 round does not happen and the IP is sold as Tortuga's was [S4]; the Series A recovers 0.1-0.3x, or $2-5M against $18M [S34]. Signposts of the unverified bear case: contracts priced per robot and a hiring freeze [S34].

**Assumptions that matter most, ranked.** First, the price basis: per-robot pricing gives $1.96M of unverified 2027 revenue on 206 robots, per-acre pricing $11.4M, a 5.8x swing [S34]. Second, acres per robot-season: 4.5 versus 5.8 acres moves unverified 2027 revenue 29% and unit payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons [S34]. Third, unit cost: $48,000 versus the unverified $31,000 target changes fleet capex per dollar of revenue by 35% [S34]. Fourth, the exit multiple: 2x to 5x sales moves Series A proceeds from $15.0M to $37.4M on unverified figures [S34]. Fifth, the H-2A wage floor: California's entry rate is $16.45 after a 17.6% cut and Florida's $12.47 after a 23.2% cut, and further cuts would stretch the 14% pilot conversion [S25][S34]. Capital need is constant: unverified 2030 revenue of $51.3M requires $57.6M of fleet capex, $39.6M beyond this round, across 5,400 acres that are 12% of California's 43,726 [S1][S34].

**Position sizing: zero.** At the base case the $18M returns 1.2x, so a 3x outcome would need a $36M post-money rather than $90M on unverified figures [S34]. Re-underwriting on the unverified figures would require a starter check with reserves covering the remaining $39.6M of fleet capex [S34].

## The one diligence question

**The one question:** What is the contracted price per acre harvested, and the documented acres one robot serves in a season? This single item swings unverified 2027 revenue five-fold, from $1.96M on 206 robots at $9,500 per robot-season to $11.4M at $9,500 per acre over 5.8 acres, and with it unit payback from 2.7 to 2.1 seasons [S34]. Resolve it from signed 2027 grower contracts, invoices from the two paid deployments and 2026 robot-hour telematics; if the contracts show a per-robot price, the unverified $90M post is unsupportable [S34].

## Three takeaways

1. The unit economics do not reconcile: a $48,000 robot against $9,500 of unverified revenue per season is a 5.05-season payback at a 100% margin and 12.3 seasons at the stated 41%, not the claimed 2.1 [S34].

2. The substitute got cheaper: California's entry-level H-2A wage fell 17.6% to $16.45 an hour and Florida's 23.2% to $12.47, with 254,688 certifications in H1 FY2026 on pace for 435,000 [S25][S27].

3. The category's best-capitalised commercial player died: Advanced Farm, with $34.2M raised and Driscoll's and Naturipe deployments, ceased operations in July 2025, and the ask is 28.1x unverified ARR against 1.6x for listed ag-equipment peers [S5][S6][S33][S34][S7].
